blocks.busolt-s02-001: Everything acts according to certain rules, which are either 1. General or necessary ones, which are used in every respect and are needed without looking particularly at this or that object. Without these no use of the understanding is possible at all; or 2.) Particular ones, or those which, in particular respects, take account of this or that object. The former rules are unchangeable, the others are changed arbitrarily: for everything particular is contingent. Without the particular, the use of the understanding is possible only in a certain science. For the understanding is properly the faculty of rules. The senses, by contrast, are the faculty of intuition. E.g. in mathematics one can comprehend, without using the eyes or instruments, that a triangle has three sides and just as many angles; but if one wants to know how a triangle is measured, then the use of the eyes is necessarily required for it. The student learns mathematics as it can be comprehended through the understanding, the surveyor as it can be comprehended through the senses, and so both act according to particular rules. Natural powers one observes before one knows them. Acquired powers one must know before their use. The animals, inanimate nature, act according to laws, according to rules, without being conscious of them. To human beings too they are often unknown, although he acts according to them. One acts according to natural rules:
blocks.busolt-s02-002: 1.) Because they are already in nature.
blocks.busolt-s02-003: 2.) From imitation, where the exercise takes place without knowledge of the rules.
blocks.busolt-s02-004: 3.) Through one's own use and exercise; here we often err, but through this we attain skill. Habitual faults excepted. Logic is the science of the rules of the use of the understanding and of reason
blocks.busolt-s02-005: Here below there is found in us the faculty of acting, and from this natural logic arises. For logic is the science of rules. In the beginning the human being acts according to rules of which he is not conscious; so for that long he has a natural logic; when he reaches maturer age he corrects this through rules, and thus artificial logic arises. Thus someone speaks German and afterwards acquires rules from a German grammar. But grammar is only a discipline, logic a science; doctrine. The difference between discipline and science or doctrine is this: with the former one cannot know why something is so and not otherwise, with the latter, however, one has an inner proof of it. With the former we consult experience, with the latter the understanding alone; the former is particular, the latter general; the first is called Scientia empirica, the other Scientia scientifica. The human being has powers, some of which serve to create materials, others to order them. The first is done by sensibility, the other by reason and the power of judgment.
blocks.busolt-s02-006: Artificial logic now (for it is of this that we are speaking here) deals with general rules, hence with those that must be used in all sciences and in the judging of all objects. It accordingly separates off everything contingent, everything particular, and thus abstracts also from the difference of objects. It selects only the form but not the matter or content of things. In every cognition one must distinguish the material, e.g. when bodies are heavy, they are driven by others; and the formal, e.g. if God is just, he punishes evil actions. Matter is the object of the cognition, form the way in which we cognize the objects. E.g. physics cognizes the objects of outer sense, psychology however those of inner sense. Both we cognize empirically; this is the form, which is thus the same in both. Accordingly logic, in this consideration, is the science of the form of the understanding. Its rules are therefore a priori, i.e. its general rules accordingly have reason as their principles, whereas grammar, and every other empirical science, have rules a posteriori, i.e. those that have experience as their principles. Experience teaches us how a thing actually is, reason however how it must be, or whence, accordingly, it is. That water is fluid, e.g., experience teaches, but whence it is fluid, reason teaches. How human beings act morally we see from experience, how they ought to act we see from reason. All our cognitions have two sources, the senses and the understanding; both together make up the cognitive faculty. This cognizing is called cognoscere. The senses give the matter for thinking, the understanding however thinks. The senses give the representation, the understanding the rule. The rules of cognition are either
blocks.busolt-s02-007: 1.) Rules of sensibility, and that is called aesthetic, from αἰσθητός, instrumentum sensorium, or
blocks.busolt-s02-008: 2.) Rules of the understanding, and that is called logic. This logic contains the rules of all cognitions and differs from aesthetic in this way, that in it everything is taken from reason and is comprehended, whereas the latter is grounded on experience and reason. Logic is thus called the doctrine of reason, aesthetic the doctrine of taste.
blocks.busolt-s02-009: All sciences that set forth rules are either 1. Canon, or a sum total of rules a priori that teach us to judge whether something accords with reason or not; or 2. Organon, or a sum total of rules that serve for the perfecting of this or that science.
blocks.busolt-s02-010: General logic, is it now a canon or an organon? If it is to be an organon, it would have to give us an instruction on how, e.g., mathematics or metaphysics could be brought to greater perfection. But this it does not do; rather its object is merely the form of the understanding, which must be the same for all and every object. Its object is therefore general, hence it is also no science; for every science has a particular object. Every science therefore also extends our cognitions; logic, however, only corrects them. General logic is therefore also not organon, nor norma, for every norm is grounded on experience. In that case it may also be called norm a priori. An organon also takes place only when a science has already been invented and brought to a certain height, so that it now perfects itself, as, e.g., Bacon of Verulam wrote an Organon scientiarum, where among other things he gives instructions on how physics could be brought to a high degree. Logic is rather a canon, i.e. it contains rules that are grounded solely on the understanding, and also can be demonstrated only a priori. The examples in logic are taken from the general use of the understanding in common life. It is therefore the propaedeutic of all sciences. Aesthetic is not organon. For otherwise it would follow that one could learn to be witty; nor is it canon; for it does not set forth rules a priori; rather it is a critique or acquaintance with rules, and indeed with the most general ones for forming taste. It accordingly puts us in a position to judge a product of utility
blocks.busolt-s02-011: properly. Remark: Canon is doctrina demonstrabilis and serves for the judication, organon for the construction of cognitions; hence they invent nothing, logic is accordingly not ars heuristica, or art of inventing. It would therefore be excellently useful even to the power of invention, for it orders it and alters it; what is invented it separates off. Aesthetic is the doctrine of the sensible power of judgment, whether a work of genius, or something else, pleases or not. It is thus the sensible cognitive power, as taste is the sensible power of judging. In taste, experiment and experience are always necessary: for even if a piece is sometimes composed according to all the rules of the art of music, it nevertheless does not please; rather Plurima vota valent. Aesthetic can also contain only empirical rules; i.e. rules a posteriori, and one could in such a way say that it is the critique of the beautiful: for although it depends here on experience, the critic can nevertheless adduce grounds why this or that pleases or displeases. Yet there is something that a poet says: malo convivis quam coquis placere, fercula mea.
blocks.busolt-s02-012: In logic one must mix in no foreign science; thus, e.g., empirical psychology does not belong in logic: for this is the doctrine of the phenomena of the human soul, or it sets forth general rules of the actual procedure of the human soul. Above all, logic does not teach how we actually proceed, but how we ought to proceed. This is shown already by the word rule itself: for a rule is the condition under which something ought to be produced. We divide the rules of the understanding into subjective, from the actual procedure of the understanding; into objective, from the correct rules according to which one ought to proceed. Logic is a doctrine of the general laws of the understanding in general. It looks only to the form of the understanding in regard to an object, not to its content, e.g. whether an inference has been made according to the laws of inference. The logical use of the understanding is either general, and that is called sensus communis, sana ratio, bon sens, i.e. one can thereby comprehend something straightforwardly, and this common understanding is the so-called middling understanding. That is, if everyone had an equal amount of understanding, there would be just as much understanding among human beings as there is now, when it is distributed so unequally by nature; yet everyone has enough of it, and no one complains of a lack of understanding, for only with his understanding can he measure the boundaries of the understanding. In recent times one appeals to this healthy understanding as if to a divine revelation, and one believes oneself entitled not to practise further in reflection and to take no pains, because anyone could easily see it anyway. Or 2. Speculative: the difference between the common and the speculative understanding; what matters is that the speculative understanding cognizes things in abstracto, the common in concreto, e.g. the rule from natural right: Casum sentit dominus, the speculative understanding understands without application to this or that particular case of common life. The common understanding, however, must first have examples and proofs. Remark: One can appeal to healthy understanding only when something can be cognized in concreto. The speculative understanding must seek to accommodate itself to the common, i.e. it must make comprehensible in concreto what it has cognized in abstracto, and this is called popularity. This very thing is a proof that our speculative cognition is clear and distinct. According to this twofold use of the understanding logic is divided into the natural and the speculative. Logic proper is the doctrine of the speculative use of the understanding: for everyone already has the natural one himself; it is also speculative for this reason, that it sets forth rules in abstracto.
blocks.busolt-s02-013: Among the Aristotelians logic was distinguished into analytic and dialectic, i.e. according to the author's explanation, into the logic 1. of certain and 2. of probable cognition. But in this way one cannot distinguish them completely enough: for in this way both have truth as their object and they differ only in regard to certainty, in that one presents the one through insufficient, the other through sufficient grounds. The proper explanation of analytic and dialectic should be this: Analytic is the logic of truth, dialectic is the logic of illusion. What now is logic according to this explanation, is it analytic or dialectic? Considered as canon it is an analytic, and as organon a dialectic. If one regards logic, considered as organon, as the logic of truth, then an advocate becomes a pettifogger, a philosopher a sophist, for one judges in such a way about objects according to general rules, without knowing the object itself, as, e.g., recently disputations etc. etc. were all presented in mathematical order. The form was accordingly preserved. The matter, however, was presented falsely. Yet the exercise in the logic of illusion is not to be censured. Logic is called doctrine of reason, but not in regard to the order of its presentation: for every science must be presented in accordance with reason, because it has reason for its object. Instead of doctrine of reason one could also call it doctrine of the understanding: for we need the understanding for all objects, reason, however, not. One must not abstract entirely in logic, but one may also make excursions into psychology and into the rules in concreto: inasmuch as logic is properly the doctrine of the border-neighbourhood of reason with sensibility, psychology and history. Logic is the canon of reason.
blocks.busolt-s03-001: Aristotle was the first logician, he is the father of logic: His logic is a product of great acuteness. The Scholastics accepted his doctrines and sought to elevate logic above all else, but they gained nothing thereby. Bacon of Verulam also gave himself some trouble in logic. Descartes did the same in his book de methodo. Malebranche writes in his work Recherches de la vérité more metaphysics than logic. Von Tschirnhausen writes Medicinam mentis et corporis mathematice illustratur, which is highly to be recommended. Locke and Leibniz also caused a great deal in logic. Wolff's logic is the best; most of these men did not set the proper limits to logic. It is, so to speak, the anatomy of the understanding. Crusius also pleases, but only his adherents. Lambert's Organon contains a multitude of insights.
blocks.busolt-s04-001: This is clear: for the form of the understanding is more important than the content, whereas a logical error is the very worst: for one does not merely make it; rather one also makes it a rule for oneself to sin. It also has a general utility when it is presented popularly. All cognition is accordingly divided
blocks.busolt-s04-002: 1.) Into Cognitionem ex datis i.e. cognitio a posteriori.
blocks.busolt-s04-003: 2.) Into Cognitionem ex principiis i.e. cognitio a priori or cognitions of reason antequam nobis data sunt.
blocks.busolt-s04-004: Cognitio ex datis is when an object is given to us, e.g. one that we have from the narration of others, e.g. the motion of the stars; but whoever knows how to state why an eclipse of the sun arose just at that time, proves ex principiis. Cognitio a posteriori is the empirical; cognitio a priori is the speculative cognition of reason. This we have either 1. from concepts, i.e. philosophical cognition
blocks.busolt-s04-005: 2. From construction, that is mathematical cognition. Mathematics and philosophy therefore differ greatly: for philosophy is cognized from concepts, mathematics from the construction of concepts. Both, however, are not distinguished according to the object. For philosophy too has magnitudes as its object. Both are cognitions of reason, and indeed both speculative; the difference lies in this, that the one rests on concepts, the other on the construction of concepts. E.g. if I wanted to reflect on a triangle, how great the angle is that contains all three in itself, I would find out nothing philosophically in order to have a correct concept of it. I must therefore construct the concepts, i.e. I must see the things in the singular coram intuitu. Intuitus a priori is when I do not think and draw the figure from experience. Intuitus empiricus, however, when I make the figure from experience. Mathematics has to do with the intuitus a priori. Otherwise one is accustomed to distinguish philosophy and mathematics according to the object, by saying that philosophy deals with qualities, mathematics with quantities. This difference, however, is incorrect, for philosophy as well as mathematics deal with magnitudes, mathematics however especially, because I can construct a concept only according to magnitude. Philosophy is a science, and must make up a system. It is therefore the system of all speculative cognition from concepts. Our thinking is properly a cognition through concepts, or a discursive cognition. The senses, however, give us only cognition through intuition, or intuitive cognitions. For him who has the former one could call a philosopher, but him who has the other a man of healthy understanding. Philosophy is not practical, but is the knowledge of the laws of reason. The laws according to which we proceed are
blocks.busolt-s04-006: 1.) Rules of skill, i.e. political laws.
blocks.busolt-s04-007: 2.) Rules of wisdom, i.e. moral laws.
blocks.busolt-s04-008: In philosophy one must distinguish objective and subjective cognition. Objectively this cognition can be a cognition of reason
blocks.busolt-s04-009: a priori; subjectively philosophy can be nothing but a historical cognition. Philosophy therefore cognizes ex conceptu, mathematics ex intuitu. In philosophy an intuitus can only be an example, whereas in mathematics an intuitus is what is essential; hence Wolff errs when in his Auszug of all the mathematical sciences he gives, of similarity, a thoroughly speculative definition. Euclid does quite otherwise, who goes at once to the application. Philosophical cognition is accordingly discursive, mathematical intuitive. Philosophy cannot be learned by heart, and a philosopher can be no adherent of a particular sect; for in that way he will learn philosophy, but not philosophizing; in mathematics, on the other hand, one can follow the utility, the necessity of another theorem, since in mathematics, as an intuitive science, one can convince oneself through the guiding thread of intuition whether this or that has been correctly judged; whereas in philosophy, as a discursive science, this guiding thread is lacking. When one finds qui dicunt academia, it means the Platonists, qui dicunt Porticus means Stoics. When one finds qui dicunt horti, it means the Epicureans.
blocks.busolt-s04-010: Philosophy is a speculative cognition of reason according to rules in abstracto. It must be a system, that is: everything in it must be presented according to a lawful order, for through aesthetic the system is distinguished from the aggregate, in which everything is thrown together, which is also called rhapsody.
blocks.busolt-s04-011: Philosophy is a system of cognitions of reason; yet objectively it can be a cognition of reason and not subjectively: for even philosophy, which is a cognition of reason in the strictest sense, can be learned from another by hearsay; so in respect of this it is subjective, accordingly no cognition of reason. A philosopher is either a practical one, i.e. one who through concepts is master over his passions, or a theoretical one, who is the lawgiver or rather law-expounder of human reason. The natural scientist is no philosopher, for he uses reason as much as he can, upon natural objects, whereas the metaphysician lets his reason, as it were, contemplate itself, and therefore rightly bears the name philosopher. He is a legislator of humanity, a sophist on the other hand a leguleius of it.
blocks.busolt-s05-001: Here cognition in general is spoken of. Logic itself deals with representations, but not with those of which we are not conscious, i.e. obscure ones, but with clear ones, i.e. with those of which we have a consciousness. Every cognition has an object and can therefore be considered in a twofold way: namely
blocks.busolt-s05-002: 1.) In relation to the object, that is the material.
blocks.busolt-s05-003: 2.) In relation to the form of the understanding, i.e. the formal of cognition.
blocks.busolt-s05-004: In logic one abstracts from the object, and looks to the form of the understanding, i.e. modus cognoscendi. This formal of cognition is now again:
blocks.busolt-s05-008: 1. Subjective, i.e. sensation; it is the alteration of the state in the subject.
blocks.busolt-s05-009: 2. Objective, i.e. cognition; it reflects the representation onto the object.
blocks.busolt-s05-010: Sensation can be communicated only to him who has or has had it, hence nothing regular can be established about it either in logic or in aesthetic, because a subject always remains distinct from others, and so too sensation. Every representation is always cognition as intuition: in such a way the representations are
blocks.busolt-s05-013: 1.) Intuition goes to a single object, insofar as it is distinguished from others,
blocks.busolt-s05-014: 2.) Concepts go to something general, for they make the particular general. From such divisions there arise then;
blocks.busolt-s05-015: a) Aesthetic, i.e. that discipline which sets forth the rule of perfection from the representations of intuiting.
blocks.busolt-s05-016: b) Logic is that science which sets forth the rules of perfection from the representations of the understanding.
blocks.busolt-s05-017: Logic accordingly has to do with clear representations, i.e. with such concepts of which we are conscious, and these we again divide into distinct and indistinct ones.
blocks.busolt-s05-018: A distinct concept is that according to which we cognize the manifold that a thing contains, e.g. in the concept of virtue I think three things
blocks.busolt-s05-021: 3.) Mastery over the desires and passions.
blocks.busolt-s05-022: If one has merely a concept of the whole but not of the parts, then the concept is called indeed a clear one, but indistinct; one does not rightly call it confused; for confusion is opposed to order, but not to distinctness. All cognitions one attains through order, i.e. per reductionem idearum subactis quosdam titulos. Between distinct and confused there is still an intermediate thing, namely simple. A simple representation is that in which no manifoldness is contained. E.g. of a single book I cannot say that it lies in disorder. The distinctness of intuition does not take place without concepts of the parts. – – The distinctness of concepts is not possible otherwise than that one at the same time cognizes and distinguishes the manifold. Philosophy is concerned with halting our understanding, in order to resolve our general concepts and to show us the whole store of our cognition. Est enim vt aiebat Socrates; Philosophia cognitionem nostrarum, quasi quaedam obstetrix non mater.
blocks.busolt-s05-023: Thus we learn in philosophy the difference between pride, haughtiness, arrogance, although we already beforehand obtain some concepts of these. But in philosophy clear concepts are made out of obscure ones, distinct out of clear ones, and a consciousness of our cognition is, as it were, imparted to us in it. The difference between logical and aesthetic representations consists in this,
blocks.busolt-s05-024: 1.) The aesthetic representation is the representation through the senses or the imagination; this imagination belongs, as it were, with the senses, it is their copyist, it is the source of intuition.
blocks.busolt-s05-025: 2.) The logical representation is the representation through the understanding, and to think therefore means to cognize through concepts.
blocks.busolt-s05-026: The first kind of representation is also called the sensible cognitive faculty, or the lower power of the soul, whereas the second kind is the upper power of the soul.
blocks.busolt-s05-027: Reason stands in relation to the understanding as the understanding does to the senses; both kinds are necessary for a concept, and otherwise no concept can be produced. The aesthetic perfections are either essential, i.e. the conformity of the sensible with the logical, or intellectual: a piece cannot please with the wittiest ideas if one cannot find the agreement of the whole imagination with the theme. From just this essential perfection arises the Sensus publicus, the general taste: for this is the faculty of choice according to the general laws of sensibility, or the aesthetic perfections are also contingent ones. These one cannot determine, for they go to the subject.
blocks.busolt-s05-028: The general and particular laws of aesthetic.
blocks.busolt-s05-029: The general laws are possible with regard to intuition. For in the judging of the beautiful, which is investigated in aesthetic (whereas in logic the true), intuition is the principal, sensation the accessorium. Intuition cannot be shared; sensations, too, cannot be imparted; if it happens, it happens through likenesses. The private laws rest on the different sensations of each. Sensations are certain alterations of our state through which all our cognitive powers are enlivened and exerted. Taste is the faculty of the sensible power of judging according to general laws of sensibility. Feeling is the faculty of sensation according to private laws of sensibility.
blocks.busolt-s05-030: From this arises the mixture of our cognitions out of sensations and concepts. If our cognition is separated from all sensations, then it is pure. The purer the cognition, the less it is sensation. The stronger the sensation, the less, and correctly, pure is the cognition. Accordingly we must not let ourselves be swept away by the dazzling magic power of the senses, but first ground the cognition itself, and then build the sensation upon it, and so the proper edification arises. Sensations take one by surprise, cognition comes gradually; those are something transitory, this something lasting. The general aesthetic perfection consists in charm and emotion. (Delinementum est mentis concussio.) Attrahit delinementum, nos quoad contemplandum longius objectum detinent. Convolvit concussio animum nobisque quasi quendam horrorem infundit. Mens delinementa sentit, quandam animae voluptatem, atque in objectum quasi acquiescit. Concussio est tamquam animae aliqua actio. Delinemento, ne ob dulce animis condimentum fastidium moveat, concussionis atque commutationis aliquid admisceatur, conquassatio haec est, habitur quidam dolor, puncto temporis inquinatam voluptatem resolvitur.
blocks.busolt-s05-031: On the manifold kinds of cognitions. A rational cognition and a cognition of reason are very different. A rational cognition is when it is merely in accordance with reason, i.e. one that the human being can see through his reason, and cognitions of reason are those that are derived from reason; in every science one requires such. The author says that a learned cognition and a philosophical cognition would be one and the same, but they are very different. For all our cognition is either historical or cognition of reason; the latter must be speculative from concepts if it is to be philosophy. To historical cognition belongs literature, which comes from litterator, i.e. one who knows the books; he is a philologist if he is a critic and knows especially the ancient languages. It is already a great degree of such a learned man, up to the polyhistor, who is, as it were, a giant of learnedness. He does not learn philosophy and mathematics, but already knows them historically. He has a knowledge of books and himself judges the ancient philosophers. They are nothing but half-learned; they know historically what great men have said. But the ground is lacking to them. By the way of imitation I can become no philosopher; I must owe nothing to others, but through them only improve their concepts. A philosopher is no learned man, for in philosophy one does not need to be instructed. A learned man is one who has been taught. They know nothing other than what has been taught to them. Philosophy and mathematics, however, I can have from myself; only history can I learn. A learned man is eruditus, not litteratus; the latter is one who can read and write. Mathematics is no learnedness, but a cognition of reason; philosophy is also a cognition of reason; but in philosophy one can speak discursively, in mathematics intuitively. A mathematical chatterer one cannot conceive, but a philosophical one one can, namely if one learns the expressions that they have all used and adds something new. They put sciences on display. The fine sciences are no learnedness. It is good when a poet, an orator, is a learned man, but what is beautiful, what moves, he must have from reason. They are arts and not sciences. What matters in them is not to know something, but to be able. Wit, taste, genius belong to it. Aesthetic is a critique of art. Logical perfection makes the particular general, goes from intuition to concepts. Aesthetic perfection, by contrast, the reverse. The greatest perfection is the combination of logical perfection with the aesthetic, since only then does one become comprehending and comprehensible. All cognition that concerns our understanding relates to the object, all cognition that concerns our senses relates to the subject; logic aims at cognizing the particular through general concepts. Aesthetic cognizes the general through the particular; it merely fills the soul with intuitions. Logic seeks to bring all cognition to concepts, aesthetic all to intuitions. Both must be able to be united, if I want to cognize the general in concreto. Only he can make cognition sensible who makes it intuitive. A cognition that is indeed logically perfect but not aesthetically one calls well-grounded, but dry. On the other side, a cognition is beautiful, stimulating, agreeable, engaging, but it lacks logical perfection; then it is shallow. The entertaining does not indeed make up the essential; but our cognition loses nevertheless if it is lacking. Lack of it is opposed to beauty, and on the other side ugliness. The first one calls dryness. Affectation is an ugliness. One can narrate the most cruel representations and yet clothe them beautifully; only not disgust, this cannot be hidden by any art.
blocks.busolt-s06-001: Cognition one calls the whole extent of the concept that someone reaches of a thing and that comprehends in itself all the propositions that have become known to him of it; the greater the number of these propositions, the more detailed and complete, the more sharply one can prove them, the more certain, and the more frequent the application these propositions admit to cases that occur, the more useful is our cognition. The perfection of cognition specifies itself into quality and quantity. The perfection of cognition in regard to quality is one and the same in all cognitions; in regard to quantity, it depends in each object on the multitude and the degree. In regard to quality the perfection of cognition is theoretical and practical. The first relates to the understanding, the other to the will. The first is considered only in logic, the other determines actions.
blocks.busolt-s06-002: Theoretical cognition is the fruit of speculation or of reflection; the practical grows from the applications that one finds occasion to make in practice. The former is obtained by laying certain concepts at the ground, drawing consequences from them, and then setting inferences upon inferences; the latter consists in a collection of experiences and the consequences drawn from them. Theoretical perfection is either aesthetic or logical
blocks.busolt-s06-004: a.) The matter (obiectum) which consists in truth, and thus in regard to quality.
blocks.busolt-s06-005: b.) The form (modum cognoscendi) which consists:
blocks.busolt-s06-006: aa.) In generality, that we cognize everything from concepts.
blocks.busolt-s06-007: bb.) In distinctness, that we make these abstract concepts representable in concreto
blocks.busolt-s06-009: a.) The material, this is here sensation,
blocks.busolt-s06-011: aa.) Manifoldness; the opposite of this is logical generality. It must in its definitions send away everything else, abbreviate everything, whereas the former extends and expands everything, through synonyms etc. etc.
blocks.busolt-s06-012: bb.) Unity: for all these expansions must nevertheless all make up a whole, e.g. the description of spring from the mouth of the poet and of the astronomer.
blocks.busolt-s06-013: The essential of concepts is generality; the essential of intuition, manifoldness; aesthetic perfection as to form pairs best with logic. Logical perfection combined with the aesthetic one calls conciseness. Aesthetic and logic combined means: manifoldness. Manifoldness and generality are so combined that neither does injury to the other
blocks.busolt-s06-014: Distinctness in logic is what liveliness is in aesthetic. The livelier the representation, the more emotion it arouses, but the less I cognize. It is thus the enlivening of the senses. Distinctness, however, occupies us with the object
blocks.busolt-s06-016: 1.) Taste, and this is the form,
blocks.busolt-s06-017: 2.) Feeling, and that is the matter: for charm and emotion belong to it.
blocks.busolt-s06-018: A practical perfection of logic is not possible, for it would be the movement of willing; this is set forth in morals. The art of the beautiful is sometimes applicable. To use pictorial beauty from nature in poetry is not well applied. For no art attains the beauties of nature by depicting and describing. We seem, as it were, to want to compete with nature, whether we can also make such an intuitive concept as would follow nature; for this reason Haller is censured in his Swiss poems. With regard to human actions art can not only attain them but also surpass them; e.g. in those we cannot be so beheld with our depicting as in intuition, e.g. Milton described the globe and its fall magnificently. Up to the highest being we must not venture with pictorial beauties; hence an astronomer could depict God better than a poet, for the first says: Behold, so great are the works of the LORD; whereas the other with his sensible images would depict too lowly, since sensibility cannot be thought at all in the concept of God.
blocks.busolt-s07-001: Deficiencies (defectus) must be well distinguished from faults (vitiis). In a deficiency the cognition is still correct, it is only lacking to me. In a fault, however, it is erroneous. E.g. in geography I can omit important cities, so this is a deficiency, but if I place a place falsely, this is a fault. The deficiency can be made good, the fault, however, must first be reduced to a deficiency. An error is a hindrance of true cognition; before one confirms oneself in error, one had better remain in a degree of ignorance.
blocks.busolt-s08-001: A horizon is in general a circle that bounds all objects that we can see. Here the horizon is: Congruentia cognitionis cum terminis perfectionis humanae. This horizon divides into the logical, according to the cognitive faculty, and the practical, according to utility. The logical horizon must precede the determination of the practical: for utility follows only upon cognition. Here I must first not ask about utility. Utilities often hide themselves for a very long time. When Archimedes found the ratio of the cone to the cylinder, it would have been difficult for him to state its utility; long afterwards it showed itself in common life. The practical part does not belong to logic, so nothing more will be said of it. As to the logical, however, we divide it:
blocks.busolt-s08-002: 1.) Into the general horizon of the human understanding in general. This can be determined only through deep metaphysical investigations.
blocks.busolt-s08-003: 2.) Into the practical horizon of this or that aim. Here the difference is to be noted:
blocks.busolt-s08-004: a.) How I determine the horizon of my
blocks.busolt-s08-005: b.) How I determine the horizon of others' cognitions. I can determine the horizon
blocks.busolt-s08-009: 4.) From the age of a human being.
blocks.busolt-s08-010: Rules for determining the horizon. One should not determine the horizon too wide from the start, e.g. in the schools one learns many things that one afterwards lets lie, such as, e.g., the oriental languages. One should therefore always determine the horizon narrow. One should also not determine one's horizon too narrow, because
blocks.busolt-s08-011: a.) Much is lost of the cognitions
blocks.busolt-s08-012: b.) Because we do not know for what we may yet use these cognitions.
blocks.busolt-s08-013: One should not change the horizon of one's cognitions too often. E.g. when a theologian becomes a jurist, and sometimes the reverse. The general logical horizon we can also determine:
blocks.busolt-s08-014: 1.) Logically or a priori, and this is the horizon of reason.
blocks.busolt-s08-016: aa.) In the case of individual objects.
blocks.busolt-s08-017: bb.) With regard to the whole human race, namely how far the sciences have risen from the beginning up to our times.
blocks.busolt-s08-018: The first, namely the horizon of reason, is determined especially in metaphysics: for in such matters one asks not how far the human understanding has gotten, but how far it could get. The horizon of reason is:
blocks.busolt-s08-019: a.) The horizon of healthy reason and
blocks.busolt-s08-020: b.) The horizon of speculative reason.
blocks.busolt-s08-021: The horizon of healthy reason is more narrowly bounded than that of the speculative. Everything is rising: natural science, natural history, mathematics, history, and one will necessarily have to cast everything into a narrower form, so that the sciences do not fall into decline merely because they have risen so high. For men would necessarily be discouraged if they were not to make the name of an inventor shine. In times of great ferment, therefore, much philosophy is needed, in order to choose the most necessary and most useful from so many sciences. To recognize ignorance one must know much, for an ignorant person does not recognize his ignorance. He cannot comprehend how he could be so lacking in knowledge of the world. The common man, e.g., takes the stars for points and believes that another person also takes them as such. The more we cognize, the more we see that we are still ignorant, that we cultivate only a small part of the great field of possible and useful sciences. In order to know one's ignorance, one must at least know an outline of the sciences, so that we recognize what we know and what we lack; we must at least know the sciences extensively. Ignorance in and for itself is something blameworthy, but not every ignorance is to be regretted; for he who is always digging behind the actions of men and seeking out their source, if he everywhere finds only self-interest, one's own good and one's own aims as the motives for actions, will in the end take virtue for a chimera, and the practice of it for folly. No one ever has perfect virtue, nor can it be practiced. Scholars who know their ignorance not infrequently become confused, e.g. Condamine, the famous French naturalist, who, on beholding the inexhaustible store of natural things in Peru, lost all desire to extend natural history. They will keep giving us more problems that we cannot solve. On the extent of knowing
blocks.busolt-s08-022: 1.) Learnedness is the sum total of all historical sciences.
blocks.busolt-s08-023: 2.) The philology of the ancient languages is the sum total of the instruments of learnedness.
blocks.busolt-s08-025: a.) A litterator, i.e. one who has book-knowledge of the ancient writings,
blocks.busolt-s08-026: b.) A linguist, if he knows the ancient languages, and indeed critically,
blocks.busolt-s08-027: c.) A humanist, if he studies the beauty of the ancient writings, and then
blocks.busolt-s08-028: d.) A belletrist, who forms his taste from the more recent writings.
blocks.busolt-s08-029: The whole of polyhistory seems to be far too great a cognition. But it is only a cognition of all the sciences. One could call it a Cyclops, because it lacks an eye, namely critical philosophy. Philosophy too is a polyhistory, but only historical philosophy. Set beside polyhistory is polymathy. The former is a cognition of all historical sciences, the latter a cognition of all sciences of reason, or of all the opinions of the philosophers. A scholar who is both together is a pansoph.
blocks.busolt-s08-030: But this requires more memory than genius. Encyclopedic skill is a dexterity in bringing the sciences into small compass. It is rhapsodic and a mere compilation, but it ought to be a system; and must therefore not be rhapsodic, but methodical. The encyclopedia brings all the sciences under one title, it indicates their genealogical tree. Such a tree is organic. The dead languages are the vehicle of polyhistory and the commerce of the fine sciences, because they
blocks.busolt-s08-031: 1.) Are the instrument of the sciences and
blocks.busolt-s09-001: To this belong pedantry and charlatanry. The word pedant comes from the Italian. A magister pedarius was one who led children and was in their company alone, and who consequently adopted manners that do not suit public life. For commonly they are wont to observe an all too anxious scrupulousness in formulas, to which a purposive punctiliousness is opposed. Charlatanry borders on pedantry. For he who possesses the former indeed has no scholastically correct knowledge, but nevertheless seeks, through the appearance of possessing it, to deceive others. Pedantry, however, presupposes scholastically correct knowledge. They approach especially popularity, in that they present knowledge that not infrequently requires deep reflection playfully and as easily comprehensible to the capacity of everyone. This is a chief character of the French. The author says: pedantry is a charlatanry. But the two are very different. The former is a learned but restricted cognition without popularity. The latter is a boasting in cognition and consists in one's seeking to bring one's own restricted skill to bear everywhere. The perfection of cognition must have a certain art of relation. It is either:
blocks.busolt-s09-002: a.) Scholastic, if it makes up a part of learnedness, or, coascendentia ad certum conditionis gradum, or,
blocks.busolt-s09-003: b.) Popular, i.e. the condescension to general concepts.
blocks.busolt-s09-004: This condescension is a skill in accommodating oneself,
blocks.busolt-s09-005: aa.) Both to the sum total, and also
blocks.busolt-s09-006: bb.) To the capacity and comprehensibility of the publici and of the multitude.
blocks.busolt-s09-007: Scholastic knowledge can be great in degree and small in application. If one wants to be popular, one must subtract something from thoroughness, detail, determinateness. Scholastic cognition has thoroughness as its essential; popularity adorns and embellishes; only thoroughness, solidity, is guided with the leading-strings of terminology. A sermon must be not only scholastically correct but also popular, and a sustained condescension belongs to it. A preacher cannot be a gallant orator. For the more dignity a matter itself has, the less ornament it requires. In general solidity is always to be preferred to popularity. For the more popular, the less solid. The skill of accommodating oneself to all the world is a knowledge of the world, and one who possesses it is called a scholar of the world. Pedantry is therefore the lack of popularity in learned cognition.
blocks.busolt-s10-001: 1.) Into guild scholars, who seek their bread through learnedness.
blocks.busolt-s10-002: 2.) Into scholars free of the guild, who use learnedness merely for pleasure.
blocks.busolt-s10-003: The former must necessarily be of more use to the world than the latter: for they see themselves compelled to reflect more deeply on the matter, since they are obliged to show their listeners the object, as it were, in various positions. The others are of course prouder: for they say that the free arts must not be used with the aim of trades.
blocks.busolt-s11-001: Truth is the agreement of cognition with the object. Appearance is contradictorily opposed to truth. On the question of general criteria the philosopher founders. They have been unable to find any general criterion of truth. A general criterion is one where a mark is provided without regard to the object itself; it must be indifferent to all objects, the explanation must here be abstracted from all differences of determinate objects; it is concerned, then, merely with the form. The general criterion of truth thus already lies in the question. He wants to have signs of truth, and this is the agreement of cognition with the object. He wants to have general marks, i.e. he wants to have a sign that applies generally to all objects, he wants to have a sign of the form. The general criterion of truth is here, then, merely formal, the agreement of cognition with the object. Logic can therefore give merely formal, not material, general criteria of truth. It gives merely a relative criterion; general material criteria of truth logic cannot give. For a cognition can be false in relation to one object but true in relation to another. Every object has its material criterion. The material criterion cannot hold of all objects. Material truth consists merely in the distinction of one object from others. Whoever, then, demands from the logician a general criterion of truth must not demand a cognition of the object, whether it is correct, nor a general criterion of truth either. The general criterion of truth in logic is an agreement of cognition with itself. This mark indirectly gives a distinction, that if a cognition is contrary to the logical form, it is certainly false, because it contradicts itself.
blocks.busolt-s11-002: Remark. The dialectical use of the understanding is the production of appearance. The formal very often deceives. E.g. A beautiful garment adorns a stupid head. On the other hand, a scholar is often hidden beneath a poor garment; it is just so with cognitions. If, of two opposed propositions, the one is false, the other is true. Whoever, then, wants to show the truth of a proposition has two ways before him. Once, he can directly prove the truth of a proposition itself; the other time, the falsity of the opposite, which happens when he correctly infers something absurd from it. For a proposition is certainly false if it has false consequences. In the first case it is called a direct, in the other an indirect et apagogic demonstration. The criteria of truth are either essential or extra-essential. They are essential if they rest in the cognition itself and agree with the highest laws of the understanding. Extra-essential, if they consist in the agreement of the general human understanding. The marks that we have of truth are therefore twofold:
blocks.busolt-s11-005: The judging a posteriori, whether a proposition that I have made according to general rules of the understanding also finds approval in everyone's understanding, cannot be dispensed with. It is the test whether a proposition agrees with the laws of the common understanding or not. Marks are not objective but subjective, they are taken from the agreement of other, particular subjects. There are therefore objective criteria of truth; these consist in the agreement of cognition with the laws of the understanding and of reason. These are not sufficient. There are two subjective criteria of truth, which must be added to the preceding, and which consist in taking together the judgment of different people. I concern myself here, then, with the agreement of the subjects. –
blocks.busolt-s11-007: 1.) I compare my knowledge that I have of objects with the cognition of other objects that have already been taken to be true. This makes a great difference in the application of the common rules of the understanding and of reason.
blocks.busolt-s11-008: 2.) I see whether the cognition of my subject agrees with the cognition of other subjects.
blocks.busolt-s11-009: In general that is true which is valid for everyone, and what has only a private validity is only an appearance. The drive to consult others in the investigation of truth is already innate in man by nature. The formal essential cognitions of truth are:
blocks.busolt-s11-010: a.) A cognition must be possible; this is a negative criterion.
blocks.busolt-s11-011: b.) A cognition must be grounded in a certain way:
blocks.busolt-s11-013: B.) As ground. As such, when it is a correct consequence from true grounds. As ground, when it is a ground of true consequences.
blocks.busolt-s11-014: The consequences can be regarded as grounds (rationes), not indeed as rationes succedendi, but cognoscendi. The possibility of the cognition must be connected with a true ground that has correct consequences, and with true consequences that have a correct ground. – Groundlessness and impossibility are signs of falsity. Groundlessness is an incomplete sign of falsity. – Impossibility is a sufficient, apodictic ground that a cognition is false. In the case of truth, on the other hand, possibility is a complete sign, but thoroughness a sufficient sign of it.
blocks.busolt-s11-015: Truth is a perfection of cognition in general. But it belongs specifically to logical cognition. It is logically also aesthetically perfect, but especially aesthetically: for it relates to the subject.
blocks.busolt-s11-016: Logical and aesthetic truth differ in this: aesthetic truth is that which agrees with the ends of sensibility. One of these two can obtain in a cognition, but not the other. E.g. One finds fault with Shakespeare for letting ghosts appear. There is here indeed no logical truth, but nevertheless aesthetic truth, for Shakespeare has the end of impressing this right upon the senses. Further, it is indeed also nothing impossible that ghosts could appear to us sensibly, even though it is not settled. For these aims of Shakespeare, however, aesthetic truth is sufficient. E.g. in Aesop's fables the animals are represented as speaking. We can think a cognition that is wholly true, also one that is wholly false, but also one that is neither true nor false. Every judgment, even if it is false, must nevertheless in some respect agree with the laws of the understanding, and also be somewhat true. It is therefore certain that in a false judgment something little is always true, even if it is insignificant compared with the false. The author gives a distinction between an exact and a crude cognition. This distinction is incorrect. For the crude is opposed by the subtle cognition. An exact cognition is one that agrees with the object in all respects and is in accordance with the end. It is called a precise cognition. A subtle one, in which there is a greater degree of cognition than the end requires, a crude cognition, in which there is a smaller degree of cognition than the end requires. E.g. The cognition of God is an exact, crude, also subtle cognition. All men must have a correct cognition of God. The degree of correctness is different in different men. A teacher e.g. must already have a subtle cognition. If, however, he thought of him as a corporeal being, i.e. if he had a crude cognition, he would be much to blame for it. Even if it is permitted to the common man. Subtle cognition is lacking in the extensive. There are sciences that demand everything precise. E.g. I go for a walk; it is better if I give the money that I want to spend on it to the poor, thereby I exercise my duty of love. One says: something is tolerabiliter true, i.e. if the error in the cognition is not considerable; or if the incorrectness of a cognition does not hinder its end. The author in § 104 makes a distinction between dogmatic and historical truths (ex datis); these are opposed to cognitions of reason (ex principiis); but not the dogmatic ones. Cognition of reason is from concepts, and is an apodictic ground, i.e. one that with the consciousness of necessity
blocks.busolt-s11-017: is connected. Ex principiis a cognition is either from concepts or from construction of concepts. The cognitions from concepts are dogmata; those, however, that are connected with intuition, i.e. when the general is cognized in intuition (in concreto), are mathemata. The first is therefore a philosophical, the other a mathematical cognition. Now for the author a multitude of dogmatic judgments are truths that are so connected that they make up a whole, a system. But this it is not. For one can take the manifold together through mere similarity. A system, however, is where the idea of the whole precedes the determination of the parts. An aggregate, however, is where the knowledge of the parts precedes the concept of the whole. Our author's explanation of system would thus be nothing other than an aggregate. I can aggregate according to similarity; not according to ideas. The author says: that a system consists of dogmatic truths, this is not right, for there are indeed other systems too, e.g. the system of nature is a historical system. All cognition that makes up an aggregate can be called a rhapsody, but that which makes up a system, a science, i.e. concept of the whole, where namely its parts taken together make up a whole. Truth is opposed to error. Error is a representation of a false cognition as a truth. We do not always make use of the laws of the understanding and of reason. How can error arise? This is a difficult question. We therefore remark:
blocks.busolt-s11-018: 1.) Error and truth occur only in reason, not in concepts or intuitions.
blocks.busolt-s11-019: 2.) Through the senses we have no judgments; only intuition. Where no judging is done, there is neither truth nor error. The senses therefore do not err either.
blocks.busolt-s11-020: 3.) The understanding does not err either in the case of concepts
blocks.busolt-s11-021: A compendious means of not erring is: not to judge at all. This means is certainly not to be recommended; nevertheless it is good if the cognition of the matter is [nicht] too greatly elevated above our cognition of the understanding; because error very easily arises from this. One can judge and yet not err, namely if one does not judge decidedly, not assertorically, but problematically; if I add to my judgment: non liquet, it is not settled. But to judge in this way is no gain for reason. I must only judge the cognition problematically at the beginning, assertorically in time. Problematic judging must precede assertoric. Those who judge problematically are called doubters; one could better call them cunctatores.
blocks.busolt-s11-022: All judgments are actions of the understanding and of reason; although they are also erroneous, we cannot nevertheless say that the understanding in itself errs. For it is the touchstone of truth. The understanding acts according to its laws at all times in agreement, and agreement is formal truth. The senses do not err in themselves. For they do not judge. Error springs from the mixing of the two. We namely do not distinguish the inference of the senses from the effects of the understanding. A force can deviate from its laws only when another mingles in. E.g. I let a stone fall from a tower; I will judge that it will fall straight down, but it is driven to the side by the wind; I will nevertheless not think that it deviated of itself, but that a second force has mingled in, which pushed it away. It is just so with the understanding and with the senses. In the case of error we appeal to the limits of reason and thereby disgrace not ourselves, but nature. This is wrong, however: for the narrow limits of reason are the causes of lack and not of error. Every error arises partly from the understanding, partly from the senses, we must therefore seek its sources in both. Insofar as it has sprung from the understanding, it is true. Error also arises at times from the understanding, so all error, as a judgment, has a partial truth. If subjective grounds are falsely held to be objective, this is an error; we confound the subjective with the constitution of the object, and then an error arises through this exchange. Here one exchanges the conditions of the understanding with the conditions of sensibility. A negative criterion of truth is therefore the certainty that one has not erred, that one has separated off the subjective grounds of holding-to-be-true. One has made use merely of the understanding, with sensibility put aside. But that seldom occurs. – For one cannot notice it, it is like an enchantment when one mingles sensibility in. E.g. When someone tells a superstitious little story, he says beforehand: I am not superstitious, and yet I find the little story wondrous. Meanwhile one must guard in every possible way against the influence of sensibility on the understanding, E.g. All lying is shameful, but one says, white lies are permitted. But they are not. For for the most part this happens from self-interest; this is an influence of sensibility in the use of the understanding, and here lying is just as disgraceful as otherwise. In every science such an intermixture takes place, except in mathematics, where I see everything intuitu. The author speaks of a certain unavoidable error (error invincibilis), which is as certain as that a certain ignorance is unavoidable. E.g. When the last day will come. An error is always avoidable; the best remedy is not to judge. But if I must judge something, e.g. in the things of religion, then in this case an error is at times unavoidable. In morals one must judge, but there no error is unavoidable: for it has a certain evidentia with it. In judging the things of nature, e.g. whether there are inhabitants on the moon, an unavoidable error can be present; but here I may not judge. In all things where one does not know the absolutely great we have a middle measure; what is greater than this is admired, what is smaller is despised. It is just so with the understanding: the common understanding is the middle measure among the understanding of all men, and one calls absurd what contradicts this understanding. To deny men the common understanding is an insult. Error can often be refuted by a test. – But one must seek to arrive at the causes and constitution of the error. No error is cured by being refuted, but by being explained, since otherwise one offends the honor of the reason of others. All truths are either necessary or contingent. – The necessary must be seen through reason a priori, the contingent, however, through experience. – Both are considered by logic, even if the rules of logic are necessary. Mathematics has necessary truths, and judges a priori. The practice and test, however, does not confirm the proposition; but serves for the explanation of these necessary truths, which one calls apodictic truths.
blocks.busolt-s12-001: A mark signifies a part-concept of a whole representation. It does not consider a part of the thing. Under mark Wolff wrongly understands a concept of distinction: for 2 things can indeed also have a similarity. There is therefore a mark of identity, and one of diversity; to cognize identity our understanding is already inclined of itself; to cognize diversity it must be spurred on. The marks are
blocks.busolt-s12-002: 1.) Mediate, i.e. a mark of a mark, a mark of a representation of the mark.
blocks.busolt-s12-003: 2.) Immediate, i.e. a mark of the object that does not arise through general concepts, e.g. A body is presented to me and I say it is a stone, so one asks what is a stone? It is a body that consists of very hard earth. What is earth? What is body? This is mediate. The first one calls subordinated, the other coordinated, the first make up a series, the others an aggregate, and are partial representations that belong to the whole as partes. In the series of the subordinated there must be a mark a priori that is a first mark. E.g. What is a man? a thinking being in an organic body: What is thinking? Representing through concepts. What is representing? I cannot go further, this is the first mark, and such are general. The marks of the coordinated are a line without limit, but they are countable in that they make up a concept which they have of the thing. There are, secondly, negative and affirmative marks. The former is actually no part-concept of a thing, it is relative, the other a subjective mark. The negative are nothing other than representations for avoiding error. There are sciences where the negative marks make up the greatest part, e.g. natural theology. One can often have a negative mark of a thing, but not a positive one. There are further important and slight, fruitful and unfruitful, sufficient and insufficient marks. Sufficient marks are those that have the whole concept of the thing. It must hold of identity.
blocks.busolt-s12-004: The marks are either internal or external. Internal, which consider the inner constitution and properties; the sum total of all internal marks, insofar as they make up a concept, is an internal concept. All internal marks are either notae primitiuae, which belong to a thing alone, or notae deriuatiuae, where more than one mark can be posited of a thing.
blocks.busolt-s12-005: The logical essence is complexus omnium conceptuum primitiuorum. Primitive marks are essentialia. The derivative marks
blocks.busolt-s12-006: are attributa. The essentialia logica are also called constitutiua and are regarded as grounds. There are the attributa rationalia, which come from the grounds; bestandzeichen, if they do not belong to the essence of things as consequences of other marks. E.g. The three sides of the triangle are essentialia, they belong to the essence; the angles are attributa. E.g. In a body, extension and shape are constitutiua. They belong to the essence and are primitiua; on the other hand divisibility, movability, changeability are deriuatiua. Extraessentialia are either no internal marks at all and are relationes, or they are indeed internal, but they are modi, e.g. that a man is rich or poor, master or servant, are relationes. Learnedness is a modus. Clear cognitions belong to logic, but obscure ones do not, but to psychology. That a clear cognition is in us, we can know through truth, that an obscure one is in us, however, through inferences. Logic has nothing at all to do with obscure representations, clear ones must be given to it. The action by which a concept becomes clear, when it was previously obscure, is called euolutio conceptus. The making-distinct of a representation is not euolutio; but analysis, or dissection. Analysis of a concept is the concept successively led to the partial representations. Of the first logic gives us no means, but of the other it does. When the marks become clear, the whole representation becomes distinct. In the concept of the triangle I have
blocks.busolt-s12-009: 3.) Of an enclosed surface; and in this way I have a distinct representation of a triangle.
blocks.busolt-s12-010: The author speaks in § 125 of objective and speculative obscurity; but obscure is always subjective; for the object of my consideration contains in itself neither distinctness nor obscurity, but this arises merely through the representation or the concepts of some thing. To obscure representations we very often owe much. For, since through speculative reason we would very often have been plunged into artful sophistical errors, if some obscure representations had not still held us back; obscure representations are therefore not to be regarded as none at all, but as those that do not leave behind for us a sufficient concept of an object. Completudo conceptus clari consists in the totality of the marks which, taken together, form the concept of a thing. We encounter these concepts little in empirical things. Total clarity will be there only where we can also connect what we think with intuition. Subjective clarity of cognition is strength and liveliness of the understanding. All passions can well be aroused in jest, only not disgust; this is aroused quickly, but does not vanish so soon: for the other passions enliven the powers of the mind, disgust, however, strikes them down. Strength is distinguished from liveliness in that it is a liveliness of practical consequences. Liveliness is something when a thing is brought to intuition for us as if the thing were actually before me. But there is also a liveliness that is not even objectively sensible. If a thing is presented vividly it must
blocks.busolt-s12-011: 1.) Lead to interest, this is objective
blocks.busolt-s12-012: 2.) Work upon intuition, and that is subjective
blocks.busolt-s12-013: To make a concept distinct does not mean to extend a concept; but to make it distinct in all its parts through analysis; if, however, I want to know distinctly the object of which I do not yet have a distinct concept, this means to make it distinct through synthesis, or to add what intuition offers to cognition. If I know, e.g., that gold is not only yellow, malleable and of particular weight, but also that it does not rust and is resistant to fire, then my concept of gold is extended per synthesin. Distinctness per synthesin can occur empirically, i.e. through experience or a posteriori.
blocks.busolt-s12-014: One can represent things to oneself in different ways.
blocks.busolt-s12-015: 1.) To represent something to oneself through a concept.
blocks.busolt-s12-017: 3.) To cognize through the understanding, or to understand
blocks.busolt-s12-018: 4.) To have insight through rules a priori.
blocks.busolt-s12-019: 5.) To have sufficient insight into something with respect to all things.
blocks.busolt-s13-001: Extensive magnitude rests on the distinctness of coordinated marks, as an aggregate; intensive magnitude rests on the distinctness of the subordinated marks or of the marks of the marks. Extensive distinctness is completudo cognitionis, intensive distinctness is Profunditas cognitionis. Profunditas or thoroughness is the series of the subordinated marks, or of the marks of the marks. To make one's cognition perfect negatively does not mean to aggregate cognition; but only to keep off what would be a hindrance to cognition. Precision is when the marks of the thing are substituted. If the concept neither has too few marks, or is complete, nor comprehends too many marks in itself, or is precise, then it is conceptus, qui adaequat rem.
blocks.busolt-s13-002: Remark. Precision cannot be demanded in all sciences; but completeness absolutely. If, then, a concept is to be adequate to a thing, it must first be complete and afterwards precise. From this precision follows the elegance that mathematics possesses. – For if the mathematician gives a definition, it must be so suited to the thing that no rhetorical beauties occur in it. Precision is therefore in the strictest sense a logical perfection; abundance must have a permission, where it is to be admitted, and this can be given only where something happens in fauorem sensualem.
blocks.busolt-s14-001: Certainty is a sufficient consciousness of truth. It is therefore a state of our reason. Holding-to-be-true signifies the state of the mind insofar as it judges about a thing. Certainty is objective. This is certainty:
blocks.busolt-s14-003: 2.) Rational through reason, or apodictically certain. The different kinds of holding-to-be-true are:
blocks.busolt-s14-004: 1.) Opining, i.e.: when I hold a thing to be true although I know that I have no sufficient ground for it. It is neither a subjective nor an objective ground of holding-to-be-true. It is asked whether we judge here assertorically or problematically? The answer is:
blocks.busolt-s14-005: It is actually nothing other than a problematic holding-to-be-true. Opinions are not determinate declarations. It is a sign that a man thinks if he can alter his opinions, if he knows how to consider them from another side. Opinion is actually
blocks.busolt-s14-006: a consciousness of the insufficiency of one's own holding-to-be-true.
blocks.busolt-s14-007: Opining is of great use. All knowledge apart from the mathematical begins from opinions; after opinion comes the comparison of the marks and then certainty.
blocks.busolt-s14-008: 2.) Believing, this is a subjectively sufficient ground of holding-to-be-true, with the consciousness that it is objectively insufficient. Opining is neither a subjective nor an objective, believing only a subjective sufficient ground of holding-to-be-true. This believing is no objective necessity, because the other can have equally weighty grounds for not holding the thing to be true. In the beginning we must also judge with insufficient grounds: for they are a part of certainty.
blocks.busolt-s14-009: 3.) Knowing. It is a subjectively sufficient holding-to-be-true, with the certainty that it is also objectively sufficient. Believing we restrict to another's testimony; on this we can also already ground knowing. Where there are no documents, there we only believe. But even if I have quite distinct marks, I still cannot say, I know it for certain: for there can still be something insufficient. Best is the language of modesty, that one says: I believe it. In believing a practical interest always runs along with speculative cognition, which is of such a kind that no man can figure it out. The ground of holding-to-be-true through belief is often more sufficient than knowing. Remark. In opining I judge problematically, in believing assertorically, in knowing apodictically. The objectively sufficient holding-to-be-true, even though it becomes logically insufficient, is sufficient for belief in cognition without regard to the action of logical holding-to-be-true. Here the discussion is of historical belief. There is also a rational belief. If practical holding-to-be-true is necessary in a certain respect, then it is a rational belief. It is wonderful that a rational belief can take place, but through reason a man can already believe that there is a God. In speculative or philosophical cognitions one can opine, but only about empirical things. If now there are things that concern reason alone, then I cannot opine, I must have grounds, either to believe or to know. In the case of empirical things we can form opinions, because, if we pursue these, we proceed along the guiding thread of insufficient grounds and may well gradually come to certainty, and can confirm it. E.g. Of thunderstorms it was believed at first that they could have a similarity with electricity, and afterwards this was confirmed through experience.
blocks.busolt-s14-010: In mathematics we do not have opinions; but certainty. In philosophy opinions can also take place; in order to refute the opinions of others. Believing actually holds only of practical cognitions. One also uses it at times of empirical ones, e.g. whether the moon has inhabitants; certainty is either empirical or rational. Empirically I can be certain of a thing, that it exists, not that it is necessary. For the latter a rational certainty belongs, where reason decides something, there experience counts for little. E.g. If someone, after he has proved a proposition, that all angles in a triangle make up 180 degrees, wanted to take the protractor and measure it afterwards. Rational certainty is either apodictic or moral. A speculative certainty is apodictic, a practical one moral. Apodictic is the relation of cognition to the understanding. Moral is the relation to the will. Moral certainty is that which I can assert with all conscientiousness; the apodictic logical certainty is either, a Intuitive, i.e. mathematical certainty, or, b Discursive, i.e. philosophical certainty.
blocks.busolt-s14-011: This can have apodictic certainty, but not intuition. Apodictic certainty is a perfect certainty a priori; mathematical and philosophical certainties agree in this, that they are apodictic certainties; the difference lies in this, that the one is intuitive, the other discursive. Mathematical certainty brings a certain evidentia a priori with it.
blocks.busolt-s14-012: If the cognition is not objectively sufficient, then it is a persuasion. Many a one believes himself to be convinced when he is persuaded. Whoever lets himself be easily persuaded indicates a weakness of the understanding. One makes use of the expressions accepting and rejecting.
blocks.busolt-s14-013: They seem to relate to the will, and also actually relate to it: Accepting holds only where there is no apodictic certainty. If I am certain of a thing, if the grounds are sufficient, I must accept it. In order to accept something I need not be certain, and then I have accepted it with a restriction. In philosophy such acceptances are very good, and are a postponement, suspension of the judgment. This suspension is either critical or skeptical. A critical suspension is: when I postpone my judgments in order to pass them in the future. In such a suspension I say: non liquet. A skeptical suspension is: when I always leave the matter in obscurity.
blocks.busolt-s14-014: Of such a suspension one says better that he gives up his judgment, he renounces it, than that he suspends it.
blocks.busolt-s14-015: The dogmatists settle the matter at once, and do not suspend their judgment. Many a one is dogmatic by nature, commonly the proud, who have a great self-conceit. But they are also sometimes struck down again by the skeptics, who also have their self-conceit, in that they always renounce the judgment. To postpone one's judgment is useful in philosophy, and it is good if one accustoms oneself to it early. One must not straightway close one's soul. But when it comes to the practical, one must be resolute. We have two kinds of judgment,
blocks.busolt-s14-018: Judging provisionally occurs at all times, however few grounds we may have for one side or the other. E.g. When a man enters a company, everyone at once forms from his features a judgment about his character. If a man looks pale, one is wont at once to infer his sickliness. But it is faulty if one takes a provisional judgment for a determinate one, for appearance can deceive. The provisional judgments lead us to the determinate ones. Provisional judgments can also already be correct, and since out of impatience one does not apply them to the determinate ones, but takes them themselves for such, a principle arises, and this is called prejudice. From such rational provisional judgments arise the proverbs and canons of the school; one must not take these for determinate judgments.
blocks.busolt-s14-019: We have subjective grounds of judgment, one could better call them causes of judgment; if we falsely take these subjective grounds for objective, so that a vitium subreptionis arises. To this can contribute:
blocks.busolt-s14-020: a.) Opinion, the praedilection, i.e. that everything seems to us worthy of approval, and even if it is evil, nevertheless deserves excuse.
blocks.busolt-s14-021: There is also a praedilection that is an esprit du Corps, where one holds everything to be true; further there is a praedilection of the fatherland, and a praedilection of property.
blocks.busolt-s14-022: b.) Habit, this is very bad, since such people who possess it are convinced even by the most distinct proofs only through the length of time. This is found in all people, especially those who do not like to deviate from their concept. One must refrain from accustoming oneself to anything, i.e. from making it a necessity.
blocks.busolt-s14-023: One is also wont to call that a prejudice which flows from prejudice, and thus an actual prejudice is a principle. A prejudice is a principle from positive understanding or reason. The understanding or reason consists in activity, is active, has a spontaneity, the senses are passive. In prejudice reason is only passive, for it arises from inclination, this is in itself passive. We can therefore also have reason in a passive state. We have two actions of the spontaneity of the understanding.
blocks.busolt-s14-024: a.) Reflexion or reflection, when we compare our judgment with the laws of the understanding.
blocks.busolt-s14-025: b.) Investigation, when I seek at once to get to the ground of the judgments. Certain judgments require an investigation, but many do not; reflection, however, must take place with every judgment, namely whether it holds subjectively or objectively.
blocks.busolt-s14-026: At times we judge without reflection; namely, we do not reflect whether the judgment arises from the understanding, i.e. is objective, or whether the senses have been mixed in, i.e. is subjective, where inclination has slipped something in; and hence it can easily happen that human beings take subjective causes for objective ones, and then prejudice arises, which is a propensity to take subjective causes for objective ones; a prejudice is found nowhere else than where there is a propension; it is propensio ad iudicia ex caußis subiectivis. Such a prejudice arises from imitation, inclination, habit. Imitation takes place not only among children but also among older people. To this belong the proverbs of the rabble, the maxims of learned people and poets, the canons of the school.
blocks.busolt-s14-027: Precipitancy is a defect of the reflection of the understanding; prejudice happens through a propensity, not through precipitancy. The propensity that has arisen from the new habit makes the prejudices into a necessity. There are
blocks.busolt-s14-028: a. Prejudices of authority. This is grounded on the high esteem we have for others. Authority applies either to the person, or to the high esteem we have for the multitude, and to what everyone says, it is good. Furthermore we also ground a correctness on it. The judgment of the multitude is a criterion of truth: for since there are different subjects in the multitude, but the judgment of the multitude must be subjective, i.e. they must all agree in one, we therefore accept the judgment as correct.
blocks.busolt-s14-029: b.) The prejudice of antiquity. From the end of the previous century until now the prejudice of novelties prevailed.
blocks.busolt-s14-030: Now, however, people want once again to extol the old writings. Fontenelle published a work on ancient and modern writers, in which he says that we must not give the ancients any precedence: for we are all made of one stuff. He says that we still have this advantage over them, that we have their writings as preliminary exercises, which they would not have had. We have a prejudice about antiquity:
blocks.busolt-s14-031: a.) Because we believe that the sciences decline with the years. Nature is supposed to grow older and to deteriorate.
blocks.busolt-s14-032: b.) We take the knowledge of the ancients for scholarship and thereby esteem antiquity itself highly. But in historical matters we have much to thank the ancients for.
blocks.busolt-s14-033: c.) We take our wonder for an admiration. Wonder concerns sensibility, in that we do not expect something. Admiration concerns the object itself, namely what is excellent. It is just so with antiquity: we wonder, namely, that the ancients already thought so; in the case of a learned woman we wonder at her learning, because it is something rare, but we do not admire it. This wonder is very close to the impression of admiration.
blocks.busolt-s14-034: d.) Our high esteem for antiquity comes from this, that because the books of the ancients that still remain to us, these so few products, escaped the destructive force, we believe that what has been preserved through so long a time must certainly be the best.
blocks.busolt-s14-035: Remark. The favorable prejudice of antiquity prevails especially among the literati, who in fact busy themselves with the reading of the ancient writers. – These now believe that they find new discoveries already in the writings of the ancients. But commonly they do not find them until they have already been discovered. Thus Aristarchus is supposed already to have had the Copernican system, and in the same way people seek to prove from the word versorum the ancients' knowledge of the magnetic force.
blocks.busolt-s14-036: e.)
