Gratitude toward the ancients is likewise a ground of the favorable prejudice for them, and in truth they remain nonetheless always the heroes of scholarship and the first preparers of the ground. Thus in philosophy Aristotle, in mathematics Euclid and Archimedes are always the fathers; so too in the models of taste, and of the popularity prevailing in it, they will always remain our masters. We owe them much, therefore, and can consequently well judge them; but not condemn them; although especially in our new times this obligation is pushed too far, in that in the learning of the sciences one proposes the way of lectures rather than of reflection. Reading in the ancient writings is indeed to be recommended, but one must not thereby abandon the way of reflection.
blocks.busolt-s14-037: 1.) The envy of the learned among one another: for just as the learned have their power merely to thank the ill will of the books, in that, as it were out of weariness at the long pomp, they transfer the dominion to one alone, who makes them all equal, so it goes with regard to the ancients.
blocks.busolt-s14-038: 2.) The prejudice of novelty. Here we can believe that we shall get further than the ancients.
blocks.busolt-s14-039: 3.) The prejudice of the accepted doctrinal system. Those sciences that are grounded on a dogmatic doctrinal system are not free of such prejudices, likewise philosophy. Such a prejudice is that in which we will accept nothing, even through the best objective grounds, that is contrary to our system.
blocks.busolt-s14-041: a.) Moral, i.e. when one holds oneself alone to be of worth, but others not.
blocks.busolt-s14-042: b.) Logical, when one holds one's judgment to be decisive, but all other judgments superfluous and their contradiction a matter of indifference. One pays no attention at all to agreeing judgments.
blocks.busolt-s14-043: 5.) The prejudice of sensibility, i.e. a kind of laziness: for one gives common understanding a preference over all the sciences, one believes to settle everything through common understanding. One does not properly distinguish the popular use of the understanding from the scientific. A science also falls under suspicion if it entirely contradicts common understanding. These prejudices adduced were prejudices of confidence.
blocks.busolt-s14-044: The prejudice of distrust is when one is prepossessed against antiquity, or against novelty. Besides these there is also found a certain melancholy way of thinking, which commonly tends to set in gradually through increasing experience. It is twofold.
blocks.busolt-s14-045: a.) In the practical, that is with regard to the morals of human beings and with regard to actions. Of this the historians, e.g., can give us the very best ideas, when in all ages we become aware of such an assiduous effort of mortals to harm one another; so we become at last distrustful toward all human beings, and banish fidelity and honesty from the whole civilized world. This is called misanthropy.
blocks.busolt-s14-046: b.) In the theoretical, with regard to philosophy, that is called misology or a hatred of reason; since, namely, scholars, after they have taken so much trouble, nevertheless see themselves at last unsatisfied in the most important and most necessary questions, to which their reason does not suffice. E.g. Whence am I? What shall I be after death? A Condamine, a Rousseau can give examples of this. This prejudice mostly arises from this, that one initially imagined far too much. There is also found a prejudice against a nation. It is a common prejudice, and takes place chiefly among the French. The German nation, on the other hand, does not have it; it has rather a propensity to imitate others. There is also a prejudice of distrust against oneself. This is something rare, since one more often trusts oneself more than less. Nevertheless it does take place, and indeed in persons who could trust themselves more. Probability: Probabilitas est dimidium certitudinis; possibilis modus id est, quod gradum quendam probabilitatis habet. It goes to objective grounds. Verisimilitudo, however, to subjective ones. Although all of these are insufficient grounds, they are still always grounds of holding-to-be-true. All probabilities are a relation of truth to certainty; consequently here the ground must be compared with sufficient grounds. There can be no objective criterion of probability; honesty and sincerity
blocks.busolt-s14-047: of the witnesses seems indeed to be an objective criterion of truth, but is not; rather it only makes us attentive to the criteria of probability; for that reason they give us no rules at all by which we can judge the probable. The judging of probability is no work of the understanding, but of the power of judgment; this shows us whether it stands under the rules of the understanding or not. All observations that one makes differ among themselves, both in excessu and in defectu. – The mean of all these observations can be held to be the most probable. To give the rules of probability without distinction is wholly impossible.
blocks.busolt-s14-048: Doubt is a subjectively insufficient ground that contradicts holding-to-be-true. It is the means by which truth is weakened, but also at the same time an organon of its fortification. When the doubts are refuted, when they are removed, new doubts arise from their removal, whether it is really a step toward a nearer insight into the truth or not. Hereby I now fortify myself in the grounds of the refutation, which flow from the truth that was doubted; consequently I shall also bring this truth nearer. Both in holding-to-be-true and in objections I begin with obscure representations. Before we make objections, holding-to-be-true begins to become doubtful; one does not want to concede this or that, but yet cannot make it known to the other, and so a scruple arises. A scruple is therefore a ground of doubt insofar as it is not clearly cognized, and takes place chiefly in those who cannot bring their objections to distinctness. One finds scruples from subjective causes. These cannot be refuted, for they concern the state of mind, habit. With an objection we have to conduct ourselves in two ways:
blocks.busolt-s14-050: b.) When one answers it. A proposition that has not been doubted is called an established truth. This remains correct even after long doubts and retains a certainty. In the reason of human beings we can have subjective grounds in order to assert a thing objectively. These latter are principles. Skepticism denies all certainty to reason and holds it to be uncertain. The skeptic says: There are no objective assertions. But precisely by saying it he contradicts himself. Nothing can be determined as certain, is their universal principle. Now they do determine something, however, when they say that everyone has only subjective assertions. A certain resolve is called a maxim; this is a subjectively practical principle of reason, i.e. a resolution with regard to the object, to make use of one's reason in a certain way. E.g. I will never lie, even if I could gain very much thereby. Every method requires certain subjective rules according to which one connects cognitions, and a human being without maxims has no reliability at all. The maxims of reflection are:
blocks.busolt-s14-051: a.) The maxims of the dogmatic use, i.e. the resolve to make use of one's reason in such a way that one hopes to attain apodictic certainty. Maxima confidentia in certitudinem cognitionis humanae est dogmatica.
blocks.busolt-s14-052: b.) The maxims of the skeptical use, where one always doubts, in order to arrive at certainty. Maxima diffidentia in certitudinem cognitionis humanae est sceptica. Of both kinds there have been scholars. The skeptics also called themselves Zetetics. Of both kinds, one proved the groundlessness of the other. The school of Plato was called academia; of this there were 3 schools, of which the second fell into skepticism. Arcesilaus was its founder. There is also another school of the skeptics, who called themselves Pyrrhonists. They differed from the Academics in this, that the latter asserted that there is no truth at all; the former posited only a doubt therein, they took only a suspension. There is an unrestricted confidence, and also an unrestricted distrust, toward human reason. Katexochen dogmatic is he who has an unrestricted confidence from concepts in human reason. The opposite katexochen skeptical. The skeptical maxim wholly abolishes all utility of the use of reason, etc. The dogmatic seems at first to be of great utility, but afterwards one finds it otherwise. The critic stands between the two. This critical use of reason is to be recommended over the kinds of use of reason mentioned, because he judges only when one has sufficiently examined the sources. Criticism is always something permitted, indeed even necessary, because human cognition can come to sufficient certainty only thereby. It is only a pity that this freedom of criticism is so much abused. Criticism is not used until the understanding has come to a certain maturity.
blocks.busolt-s15-001: A hypothesis is the holding-to-be-true of a cognition, where from its sufficiency I infer its true consequences, e.g. when I know that there is fire beneath the earth. The cognition, then, which flows off from many true consequences is a hypothesis. If a ground has nothing but true consequences, then it is a true ground, but I do not yet cognize it a priori; rather a posteriori, or through a hypothesis. A hypothesis is a presupposition. A ground that has nothing but true consequences ceases to be a true opinion; it becomes certain. A hypothesis can never be brought to apodictic certainty. E.g. The system of Copernicus is only a hypothesis. From given consequences we cannot infer determinate grounds with certainty, unless it can also be shown that the consequences flow from a single ground. –
blocks.busolt-s15-002: To the perfection of a hypothesis belongs the following:
blocks.busolt-s15-003: a.) The possibility of the hypothesis must be certain: no hypothesis is apodictically certain. From this it follows that in metaphysics there are no hypotheses; in physics, on the other hand, they are necessary.
blocks.busolt-s15-004: b.) The consequence of the results derived from this assumed ground must be certain.
blocks.busolt-s15-005: c.) The sufficiency of the assumed ground for all possible consequences remains uncertain.
blocks.busolt-s15-006: d.) The unity of the assumed ground belongs to it, which constitutes the whole probability of the hypothesis. – The more subsidiary hypotheses are necessary, the more improbable is the hypothesis. To infer from the consequences to the grounds yields an insecurity, because the very same cognition can have more than one ground, and because a consequence flows from more than one ground. The correctness of such a ground one proves through the consequences, but one can never bring it to apodictic certainty.
blocks.busolt-s16-001: Complete holding-to-be-true with consciousness is called conviction. Holding-to-be-true from subjective grounds that are sufficient in practical relation is belief. Holding-to-be-true of which one does not know whether it arises from subjective or objective grounds is persuasion. An orator has chiefly the aim to persuade. Assent is to arise, even if he knows neither of objective nor of subjective sufficiency.
blocks.busolt-s16-002: One distinguishes knowing and being able thereby: what we know ought to happen but cannot carry out, of the first applies knowing, of the other being able. Strictly, not every knowing conditions a science: for this makes up a system. Nor is every being-able an art, for this is the faculty of bringing something forth according to ideas. In every science that makes up a system there is also art: for
blocks.busolt-s16-003: 1.) In every system there is one,
blocks.busolt-s16-004: 2.) It is always an art to bring something into systematic order.
blocks.busolt-s16-005: The idea is the ground of the manifold with regard to the product of minds. The artist acts according to a system, the craftsman through imitation. The artist and the scholar also have a similarity. Rhapsodies of cognitions can be very rich, and yet no system. This rests on the systematic unity of the idea of the whole. For sciences there belongs a convincing cognition of the totality of the whole, and for this the idea of the whole must go before, which determines in advance the place for each part. E.g. As was spoken at the beginning of logic, of matter and form, of canon and organon, etc. etc. It is just so with art; it comes from being-able, and differs in this from handicraft. An exercise for which skill through imitation is required is handicraft, but through ideas it is art. E.g. Is an architect an artist? Even if he works according to a plan, he is only a copyist; he has, however, an exercise according to the idea of another, which he must be able to grasp. Such a one is called a virtuoso; but he who has originality of ideas, i.e. his own genius, is an artist, and if in such a way he builds a house, he is an architect-artist. One also acts according to ideas that cannot be taught; they cannot be set out, and even if that were possible, the other could not at the same time act according to these rules. These too are arts, and not sciences, e.g. the art of arithmetic, poetry, etc. etc. There are also arts where the sciences go before. E.g. Glass-grinding according to optics. What sciences are? The sum total of cognition is either an aggregate or a system; these cognitions may be historical cognitions or cognitions of reason. Both, aggregate as well as system, are a whole. A system is that whole whose connection rests on an idea. In the aggregate the parts precede the whole; in the system, however, the idea of the whole precedes the composition of the parts. Every sum total of cognitions is called a science insofar as the cognitions make up a system; all historical cognition, as well as all autodidaxy, is always an aggregate and not a system.
blocks.busolt-s17-001: There is an apodictic and an empirical proof. One can at times prove something empirically, yet not give it apodictic certainty, e.g. whether the sea formerly stood over the dry land. Opposed to the empirical proof is the proof of reason a priori. – A proof that cannot attain apodictic certainty is an analogical proof. Both, the apodictic as well as the analogical proof, are either discursive or intuitive. The latter is proof of construction through concepts, the former through concepts. An intuitively apodictic proof cannot take place otherwise than in mathematics; for:
blocks.busolt-s17-002: 1.) It is to be an apodictic proof a priori,
blocks.busolt-s17-003: 2.) To be cognized through intuition a priori.
blocks.busolt-s17-004: To this belong not only concepts, but also construction of concepts, whereby one is capable of an intuitive concept, and this is demonstration. This, therefore, cannot take place otherwise than in mathematics. This apodictic certainty, whether it be discursive or intuitive, is called certainty of the first rank. The empirical makes up that of the second rank. The author also speaks of arbitrary truth. If something is arbitrarily true, I can take it as I will. – If something is assumed that is not objectively determined, this is arbitrary truth of a proposition, and is called position. E.g. That we count from 1 to 10, that in a circle there are 360 degrees, etc. etc. Of proofs it is now required
blocks.busolt-s17-006: b.) the connection of the proof-grounds with the cognition,
blocks.busolt-s17-007: c.) A certainty that consists in this connection.
blocks.busolt-s17-008: No immediately certain proposition is therefore a proof. The form of the grounds rests on distinctness. This can now be intuitive or discursive. The distinctness of the connection of a cognition
blocks.busolt-s17-009: or judgment with its grounds gives demonstration its discursive distinctness. If one considers a proof generaliter, one can take the probation from various grounds. I can ground it empirically; this gives no apodictic certainty. Every proof of reason must be complete. One distinguishes here also proof and proof-ground. Every proof-ground is an incomplete proof, and only the complete certainty, the distinctness of the connection with the proof-grounds, makes the proof. An empirical proof shows the truth of the proposition from actuality, as it is met with in other things. An apodictic or rational proof shows the necessity from the constitution of the thing. A proof is a distinct cognition of the correct connection of a proposition with sufficient grounds. A proof can therefore be false
blocks.busolt-s17-011: b.) In Consequentia, which mostly happens with analogical proofs.
blocks.busolt-s17-012: This consequence is the connection of the grounds with the consequences. An apodictic proof is therefore either a philosophical probation or a mathematical demonstration. An analogical proof seems at times to be apodictic, because many concepts often lie hidden in a discursive cognition. The author speaks of a provable and an unprovable cognition. The word unprovable is otherwise equivocal. For it also means groundless-unprovable. Such truths are principles, and are the immediate certainty of a thing. They are the last ground of all mediate ones and require no proof. The immediate independent certainties must necessarily contain in themselves the ground of the dependent ones. Proofs are further divided into
blocks.busolt-s17-014: b.) Indirect proofs. The former are called ostensive and the other apagogical proofs.
blocks.busolt-s17-015: The former is when one proves the truth of the proposition straightaway through weighty grounds; the other when one proves the falsity of the opposite; this is grounded on this: every proposition whose opposite is false is true.
blocks.busolt-s17-016: Apagogical proofs belong not so much to mathematics as to philosophy. A proof that has a perfect certainty
blocks.busolt-s17-017: is also called a demonstration. A demonstration is properly to be an apodictic certainty, a certainty through reason, and indeed an intuitive one, cum intuitu a priori, for if it were a posteriori, it would be empirical; all demonstration is therefore mathematical. Demonstration-mania is the affectation of bringing demonstrations into philosophy. It is also called demonstration-mania when one proves things for which no proofs are necessary. This is found chiefly in discussions. Logic presupposes a concept of experience. We prove a posteriori when we prove through experience, a priori when we prove through reason. Belief is no source of cognition. I can believe generaliter, i.e. I believe a cognition, and not a person; this happens through reason. The necessary presupposition of a cognition with practical interest is believing. We cannot believe if there is no practical interest in it. To believe something is therefore possible
blocks.busolt-s17-018: a.) Through mere reason, but also
blocks.busolt-s17-020: Here I believe a person, and this is a historical belief: rational belief is to be distinguished from reasonable belief: for historical belief too must be reasonable. A reasonable belief is that which has sufficient grounds to assume something.
blocks.busolt-s17-021: Can I believe objects of rational belief historically? If I already believe through reason, it would be ridiculous to believe historically; but if our reason does not suffice, we can believe others; yet only in mathematics, not in philosophy. On the testimony of others I can accept something only historically, and this has experience as its object. But the pronouncements of God we can believe: for with the concept of God the concept of the most perfect understanding is at the same time combined. This believing, however, still comes down to belief in human beings: for we believe those who recorded the Bible. No one can therefore give anything other than his experience; nevertheless there is an acquisition of cognitions where we also believe something on the testimony of others. This rests:
blocks.busolt-s17-022: a.) On the correctness of the testimonies,
blocks.busolt-s17-023: b.) On the sincerity of the witnesses, to say nothing more than what really happened.
blocks.busolt-s17-024: The Greeks and Romans did not look to this. E.g. Curtius is full of lies in the speeches he put into people's mouths. This principle was rather introduced among scholars only within the last 150 years. The object of historical belief is therefore experience, where through the experience of others I increase my own. We can have experience from others, we can also have experiences from ourselves. With the experiences of others we must look to competence and to the standing of the witnesses. Unbelief we can divide into a rational unbelief and a historical unbelief. A rational unbeliever could also be called morally unbelieving: for reason ultimately runs out into morality. This one is much to be censured, for he overthrows all morality. Historical unbelief, on the other hand, is not: for it has nothing other than a lack of insight into the credibility of the witnesses. Scholars have more reason to believe historically than the common man: for they ground themselves here on the reputation of the scholars. Historical unbelief therefore shows either
blocks.busolt-s17-026: b.) An evil heart, in that one declares all human beings to be liars, and in an insidious way will not believe their writings. One rejects here all sincerity, all reliability among human beings, and it is in a certain respect also unbelief in morality.
blocks.busolt-s18-001: We have a practical cognition as well as a theoretical one; the first represents how something is, the second how something ought to be; in the same way one distinguishes speculative and pragmatic cognition. The latter must contain the incentives to action. Even pragmatic cognitions, and in general every representation, if it does not at the same time contain the drive to actions, has the ground for speculation. Practical cognition is not always pragmatic. For it is not a drive that I should do it; rather only precepts are given for the case that someone wanted to carry them out. What the author further says here in this chapter does not belong to logic. A theoretical cognition can in turn be pragmatic. E.g. Whether God is just, omnipresent, etc. etc. If we know this, we seek to act rightly.
blocks.busolt-s19-001: Logic has to do merely with the understanding; operationes mentis were already rightly divided by the ancients, namely: apprehensio simplex, i.e. conceptus, iudicium et ratiocinium. Every representation we obtain through intuition, per intuitum; intuitus, however, is properly repraesentatio singularis, conceptus est repraesentatio generalis. The intuitus in mathematics is universal:
blocks.busolt-s19-002: For this intuitus occurs per constructionem conceptuum. Repraesentatio cuius mihi conscius sum, est perceptio.
blocks.busolt-s19-004: Repraesentatio subiective spectata est sensatio, sensation. Cognition is the agreement of a representation with the object. All cognition is either intuitus or conceptus. Otherwise one divides the conceptus:
blocks.busolt-s19-005: a.) into conceptum sensitivum or empiricum, where we arrive at something through intuition:
blocks.busolt-s19-006: b.) into conceptum intellectualem purum, when the representation rests merely on the understanding, and this is notio.
blocks.busolt-s19-007: The idea from the conceptus rationis, for which not even an object in experience can be given; the use of the notion, on the other hand, can be in experience, and also finds its objects here in experience. – Perceptio obiective spectata is therefore cognitio. This is either sensible or intellectual. Sensible cognitions a posteriori are called empirical. Conceptus sensitivi are where the object is given through the senses. The senses properly give no conceptus; the understanding is not intuitus; but the senses do give me the matter for the conceptus; the conceptus themselves, on the other hand, are a work of the understanding. For this is the faculty of cognizing through concepts. A conceptus can accordingly be formaliter a product of the understanding, materialiter a product of the senses.
blocks.busolt-s19-008: Remark. Of the senses, properly, not product but result is used, because the representations of the senses are not repraesentationes sentenciae, but are given.
blocks.busolt-s19-009: A conceptus can also be only intellectualis. From just this the logical form arises. Such a conceptus is called notio, et oppositum huius est conceptus sensitivus, seu potius empiricus. These notiones can be exhibited in concreto. Concepts a priori, however, of which no object can be given in concreto, are ideas; they go beyond experience, but are nevertheless no chimeras.
blocks.busolt-s19-010: The conceptus were divided into conceptus dati and factitii seu arbitrarii. Conceptus dati are the concepts that are given to me of a thing, conceptus factitii those that I have really made for myself. E.g. Every inventor of a work of art has, of the works to be produced, conceptum arbitrarium seu factitium. Conceptus dati sunt dati vel per experientiam, as conceptus coloris rubri, vel per naturam intellectus, as: the concept of substance. The representations are either a priori or empirical; we have
blocks.busolt-s19-012: b.) Conceptus factitios a posteriori; mathematics occupies itself with conceptibus factitiis. The conceptus dati are either a priori or a posteriori. These are empirical, those are pure. E.g. All concepts of colors, of taste are conceptus dati a posteriori; of virtue, a priori.
blocks.busolt-s19-013: The question of logic is how representations become concepts? It considers, therefore, the form. How does a concept arise from intuition? To this belongs
blocks.busolt-s19-014: a.) Reflexion, or attention to the manifold that is thought in the intuition.
blocks.busolt-s19-015: b.) Comparation, or the comparison of the difference and of the identity, e.g. The comparison between firs and pines, and the willows; the former have needles and the latter leaves; I thus have a concept of coniferous wood and deciduous wood; these two items belong to the positive; to the negative belongs
blocks.busolt-s19-016: c.) Abstractio, where I forget all differences and consider merely the identity.
blocks.busolt-s19-017: A concept is that which is contained in many things, the repraesentatio communis. Repraesentatio communis est quae efficit identitatem of the manifold. In the intuitus I can have more representations, in the conceptus only those that are common to various things. Usus conceptuum est vel in abstracto, vel in concreto, non vero conceptus ipse. In abstracto, when I separate a concept from all manifoldness, e.g. The concept of human beings in general.
blocks.busolt-s19-018: These are of great utility, and must precede the others: for how can I make for myself a concept of a king, e.g., if I do not first make for myself a concept of the human being. Although abstract concepts are reproached that they are not intelligible and therefore unfruitful, one answers to this: one takes from them only a common mark of many things, through which one can explain much.
blocks.busolt-s19-019: From the concept in abstracto I must gradually descend to the concept in concreto, because otherwise there is no application. Concepts are divided into high and low. The matter is that which I represent to myself in the concept. It can therefore have more or also less representation. The extension consists in that which stands under the concept, and which belongs to all the manifold. This comprises a certain magnitude of the concept, or of the extension. A concept can therefore have a larger sphere, a greater application, than another; the more I think a concept in abstracto, the greater the sphere becomes, and the content decreases. The more I think a concept in concreto, the smaller its sphere becomes, but it grows in content. A conceptus singularis has no sphere at all. A concept is called superior only in consideration and comparison of those standing under it; that standing under it is called inferior. The difference is therefore relative. A conceptus must have a sphere; the conceptus that comprehends the other in itself is called genus, that which is contained in others is called species. E.g. Iron is the species of metal. A genus, considered in another, can also be species. E.g. Metal is species of body. Further, a species can also be genus. E.g. Iron is the genus of bar iron. The difference consists in the relation; and so we always come from the genus to the species in order finally to arrive at the individuum, which one could call conceptum singularem. The greater the concept in abstracto, the greater the sphere. The conceptus summus, which has the greatest sphere, has the greatest genus, and from this first genere we come gradatim to the individuum. We can compare through the sphere only if the concepts are of one and the same kind. The difference of the species that belong under one and the same genus is differentia specifica. Differentia numerica est, si res specie eadem sunt numero diverso: Conceptus superior is called latior; inferior is called angustior. If, however, the sphere of the conceptuum is equal, i.e. if the difference of the conceptuum is infinitely small, these are conceptus reciproci. The author speaks of conceptu universali et particulari, but only the use of the conceptuum is either universal or particular. Perhaps he understands by the conceptui universali the conceptum communem; but this is every concept.
blocks.busolt-s20-001: Definitions are distinctly determined concepts; they are:
blocks.busolt-s20-004: The analytic is the definition of a given concept, in which the manifold is made distinct through dissection; the synthetic is the definition of a made concept, i.e. the arbitrary composition of the manifold whereby I make a concept of the thing distinct. To analysis belongs
blocks.busolt-s20-006: 2.) I must add nothing to it, but make it distinct to myself through analysis. According to synthesis I can say I will, e.g., that a tetrahedron be a body composed of 4 equilateral surfaces.
blocks.busolt-s20-007: Synthesis can be a priori and also a posteriori. With regard to all made concepts a definition must be given. Mathematics always begins with definitions, for it has to do merely with made concepts. It is a pure synthesis of magnitude. To be sure it also deals with space, but because that is not a made concept, it does not define it either, but assumes it as known to everyone. A synthetic definition of a thing cannot be false: for I thereby make the definitum, i.e. the concept that I have of the thing through the definition.
blocks.busolt-s20-008: A given concept is either given a priori. E.g. The concept of virtue, of space, etc. etc. or a posteriori, e.g. the concept of metal. Both are defined through analysis, e.g. a priori, when I am to define cause, I dissect the concept of cause and find that to it belongs;
blocks.busolt-s20-010: b.) A thing from which it follows; and then I define, e.g. a posteriori, when I define body, I analyze its properties, and give a complete definition. The object of the empirical concept cannot be explained, for everyone already has a complete concept of it. E.g. what earth is, what water is, etc. It does not go through analysis, because it is in vain to dissect that which can be made distinct through explication. Nor through synthesis: for I can only describe and collect concepts. We have empirically given and also empirically made concepts. Empirically given concepts can and should not be defined: for the marks are not sufficient to give the definition an exhaustive distinctness; they are perhaps only infinitely small parts of it; description, however, does take place with them. E.g. Gold I cannot define; but describe. With empirically made concepts the data are given to us from experience, and from just this we form our concept. These are found where nature is altered, e.g. the concept of a house, of a fortress.
blocks.busolt-s20-011: All definition sets out the content of the concept, the analytic as well as the synthetic; the difference between definition and description consists in this, that the first makes the concept completely distinct, the other, on the other hand, only extends it. It has to do with the content insofar as we have it. With empirically made concepts I declare, think, what I want to say. This happens through experience, not a priori; concepts a priori contain a definition. In natural science descriptions take place, and if I think several things in the same thing, this requires a declaration.
blocks.busolt-s21-001: This happens through analysis. Here the difficulty is whether the analysis is also complete? This is very rare. Nevertheless many correct consectaria can be derived from these imperfections; I can indeed know that I know nothing more; but that nothing is lacking, no one can know. An analytic definition can therefore never attain apodictic certainty. From the mathematician I can demand definition: for through the definition he makes the concept. But he can also give it.
blocks.busolt-s21-002: From the philosopher, on the other hand, I cannot demand it. For he cannot determine whether the analysis is also complete. But although he can have no complete analysis, he can nevertheless have an incomplete one, which gives him some marks. As long as such an analysis is incomplete, it is not called definition. The materials of definition are called elementary propositions, i.e. incomplete propositions toward a definition. Definitio est conceptus, qui rem adaequat. If a concept has indeed distinct marks, but too few, it is incomplete; if it has too many marks, it is not precise. A concept that has neither too few nor too many marks, i.e. that is adequate to the thing, conceptus qui adaequat rem, est definitio. A definition can therefore have completudinem, but if it does not have precision, it is nonetheless faulty, for something superfluous, not something neat and precise, is given. Opposed to precision is tautology, where the same mark occurs twice, though at times concealed. E.g. God is an infinite, eternal, omniscient being. From the concept infinite all the other properties already flow. With made concepts the definition goes first; with given ones I first make the concept distinct, I analyze it, and then I give a definition.
blocks.busolt-s21-003: A definition must be complete; but even if I cannot have complete concepts, I can still have incomplete distinct ones, and then an exposition of the elementary concepts is required. For concepts a priori a definition is indeed possible, but not necessary, though an expositio is. For concepts a posteriori there can be no definition but only description. A distinction is to be made between a nominal and a real definition. A nominal definition is one where marks are given in order to see identity and diversity. This would be an external use of the definition. A real definition, or also genetic definition, is where marks are given in order to distinguish the object from all others. This would be an internal use of the definition. The nominal and real definition given by Wolff is censured here. If a definition is to contain the difference from all possible concepts, then the marks must be entirely complete. It must therefore be both nominal and real definition. Nominal definitions are therefore not necessary unless a misunderstanding of the expression is to be feared. But with Latin terms it is necessary. These terms must be appropriate to the thing and its genesis. Etymology therefore provides special explanations of names. Explanations of names serve merely to distinguish objects from others.
blocks.busolt-s21-004: Description holds only of the empirical. Definitions that cannot be defined, insofar as they are to be objectively sufficient, are themselves an incomplete exposition and always serve also as a definition ad instantem vsum. In intellectual matters it admittedly does not work, yet here too it can be nominal, and besides be an incomplete exposition. For it is still always an approximation to the definition. For an incomplete concept et hoc sensu definitione procedere potest descriptio.
blocks.busolt-s21-005: Remark: One can best distinguish whether one has not described something if one goes backwards from experience to reason, and can explain genetically a priori what one previously had to demonstrate a posteriori. E.g. One could easily give a definition a priori of lunar eclipses as soon as one knows that the moon receives its light from the sun, and that the earth sometimes comes between the two. Chemistry composes, and that can then be defined. If, accordingly, I can resolve the object into the notas that make up its essential, that is called primary elements. In the case of definition one must ask whether the definition is true as a proposition. E.g. A human being is a human being; this is certainly true as a proposition. The soul is a thinking being. In definition one finds the greatest disagreement of philosophy. E.g. Virtue is a certain skill in certain actions. This is not correct. For
blocks.busolt-s21-006: a.) Virtue is a free action
blocks.busolt-s21-008: c.) A persistent disposition in the exercise of right.
blocks.busolt-s21-009: Of the nature of things I can say much through analysis. Analytic propositions are certainly true, but a great tautology can at times lurk in them. This is the second thing that must be examined.
blocks.busolt-s21-010: 3.) Whether the concept is also complete. This completudo arises from the confluence of all marks. Time is the order of things insofar as they follow one another.
blocks.busolt-s21-011: 4.) Whether the concept is also precise, i.e. that no more marks are added than are necessary. The superfluous marks cannot be compartes of the others.
blocks.busolt-s21-012: The cause of the lack of precision is that I transpose a mark. To say something definite means to frame the concept so that nothing more and nothing less is said than the concept contains. Thus the following belongs to definition:
blocks.busolt-s21-013: Truth, completudo and distinctness. In definition I therefore proceed thus:
blocks.busolt-s21-014: a.) I analyse my concept and seek true propositions.
blocks.busolt-s21-015: b.) The propositions must contain marks through which the concept of the definiti becomes distinct.
blocks.busolt-s21-016: c.) I collect as many marks as are necessary to bring out a complete concept
blocks.busolt-s21-017: We cannot give a definition of description, because it belongs to philosophy, and in this the first is a procedure in which one defines, the other a procedure in which one describes.
blocks.busolt-s21-018: When we try to explain much in nature, we can see from it whether the explanation has been understood; if one takes note whether the proposition can also be cognized a priori, from the very same grounds. The lunar eclipse can also be explained a priori if one knows that the earth steps between the sun and the moon. Further, if one sees whether one can also make the concept. E.g. The definition of cinnabar: mercury and sulphur sublimated give cinnabar; I can therefore make and define cinnabar. Definitio nec sit latior nec sit angustior; seu nec plus, nec minus suo in se continet definito. Definitio ne sit per circulum means: I want to explain a thing through itself, I bring the definiendum into the definition. One has a circulus vitiosus in demonstrando if I take as ground the proposition that I want to prove. One also has a definitum obscurum in definiendo if I want to use another concept, which is also obscure, for the distinctness of the other. Definitio ne sit Tautologica. E.g. The soul is a rational being which can judge; here the faculty of judging already lies under the rational being. This tautology can be explicit as well as implicit.
blocks.busolt-s22-001: This is distinguished from dissection. In logical division I look to the sphere, i.e. to the extensive application of a concept. Logical division is therefore the division of the sphere. The larger the sphere, therefore, the more it can be divided. Logical division contains the difference of various concepts insofar as they are contained under a common concept. If all disjunctive concepts taken together are equal to the sphaera conceptus, then this is a logically perfect division, e.g. Triangles are either equilateral
blocks.busolt-s22-002: or isosceles. The other concepts are called membra dividentia and must be equal to the sphaera conceptus divisi; there is a codivision and also a subdivision of a membrum. The subdivision is the division of a membrum dividens, e.g. All human beings are learned or unlearned. Codivisions are therefore divisions where I divide the concept under various divisions. They are collateral divisions, where I namely consider the concept under another sphere. The faults in logical divisions are:
blocks.busolt-s22-003: a.) When the membra dividentia are not opposed to one another
blocks.busolt-s22-004: b.) The members of the subdivision must not be brought under the members of the division, e.g. Triangles are equilateral or isosceles. This division is false. One would have to divide them thus. Triangles are either equal in all 3 sides, or unequal. The unequal ones are either isosceles, which have two equal sides, or scalene, where no side is equal. The easiest division is dichotomy. All substances are either bodies or not; this is the foundation of all logical definitions.
blocks.busolt-s23-001: We cognize something immediately or mediately, i.e. we cognize our cognitions of the object; such a mediate cognition of the cognition of the object is a judgment. I can therefore immediately through a concept only represent something, or I can through mediate cognition have a concept. I can therefore pass a judgment straight away on the object, and through this I can again pass a judgment on the cognition of the object. The relation of one cognition to another, insofar as the one is the means of the other, is the judgment.
blocks.busolt-s24-001: All judgments are brought under four titles, and divided according to four functions, namely:
blocks.busolt-s24-006: Each of these has three modi. According to quality, judgments are either affirmative or negative or infinite judgments. According to quantity, either universal or particular or singular. According to relation, either categorical or hypothetical or disjunctive. And according to modality, either problematic or assertoric or apodictic. E.g. All human beings are mortal. This judgment is, according to quality, affirmative, according to quantity, universal, according to relation, categorical, according to modality, assertoric. The judgments of the first two titles one distinguishes well enough.
blocks.busolt-s24-007: 1.) But how does one distinguish the judgment of relation? We have three kinds of relations
blocks.busolt-s24-008: a.) The subject to the predicate, i.e. categorical;
blocks.busolt-s24-009: b.) The ground to the consequence, i.e. hypothetical
blocks.busolt-s24-010: c.) The relation of the members to one another, and to the divided concept, i.e. disjunctive; the relation of the members to one another is when they are opposed. All human beings are either virtuous or vicious.
blocks.busolt-s24-012: If I hold a judgment to be possible, if I take it merely as a touchstone for what might well follow from it, then this is a problematic judgment. A judgment with consciousness of its truth is assertoric. A judgment that is necessarily true is apodictic. E.g. If I say the moon might well have inhabitants, that is problematic; if I say it has inhabitants, this is assertoric; and if I wanted to say it must have inhabitants, this is judged apodictically. In problematic judgments, therefore, the consequence remains clear, but the ground, or the one antecedent proposition, is undecided. A judgment is therefore a cognition of one cognition, or a mediate cognition of the object: for every concept is merely a cognition. E.g. Living and creatures are concepts, but human beings are living creatures is a judgment. In the definition of the judgment I cannot consider the concept alone: for there are judgments where only the relation of two concepts is necessary, that is the categorical; but in others the relation of two or more judgments is also necessary, i.e. in the hypothetical and disjunctive. The first definition, that a judgment is a cognition of a cognition, thus remains the best. That the definition of the judgment is not so evident comes from the fact that we already judge when we define.
blocks.busolt-s24-013: Remark: All actions of the understanding go to judgments, and every object that we cognize, every concept, is as it were a predicate to a possible judgment; so one can explain the understanding, which one previously explained as the faculty of concepts, as the faculty of judgments, or of rules: for the understanding is the source of rules, because every judgment is a rule and every rule a judgment; e.g. All human beings are mortal. As soon as I see a human being, this proposition is for me as it were a rule: this one too must die. This very definition of the understanding agrees with the definition that Wolff has given, namely that the understanding is the faculty of distinct representations: for only through judgments does the logical distinctness of representations arise. Accordingly, distinct representations should be discussed in connection with judgments, because a distinct concept already presupposes a judgment. A distinct concept is namely possible through a clear mark, but the representation is just as much as a predicate of a judgment. The representation of the object itself is the subject, and I therefore have the Materia sc. dati iudicii. The concept a human being is clear, a rational human being distinct: for here I represent the human being by means of the predicate rational, and so I have a judgment. Distinctness is twofold.
blocks.busolt-s24-014: a.) In the concept; this is the logical, haec respicit intellectum.
blocks.busolt-s24-015: b.) In intuition; this is the aesthetic sententia haec respicit sens us.
blocks.busolt-s24-016: We can have aesthetic distinctness of things while logical distinctness may be lacking in us. E.g. A servant stands in a palace; he has indeed a sensitive distinctness of it, but since he does not know what cornices and columns are, he lacks logical distinctness. Logical distinctness properly belongs only to the philosopher. In every judgment there occur matter and form.
blocks.busolt-s24-017: a.) Matter, i.e. the cognition by means of which I cognize an object.
blocks.busolt-s24-018: b.) The form, i.e. the relation of the cognitions. E.g. The human being is mortal; here human being and mortal are the matter, but the relation of the human being to mortality is the form.
blocks.busolt-s24-019: Because logic abstracts from all matter, only the form remains to it, and this is considered in a fourfold respect, as was just stated. The essential form of judgments consists in relation, for concepts have sphere, quality, modality, but relation is proper to the judicium. Categorical judgments lie at the ground of the others: for the hypothetical consist of two categorical judgments, of which I consider one as the ground, the other as the consequence. The disjunctive consist of several categorical judgments. The disjunctive taken together are equal to the conceptus divisus.
blocks.busolt-s24-020: Because the judicia categorica are therefore the data iudiciorum hypotheticorum et disiunctorum, the logicians regard the first as the only true judgments and said that the others could be reduced to them. When the author speaks of subject, predicate and copula, this is understood only of categorical judgments: for in hypothetical ones one must distinguish antecedens and consequens, and in disjunctive ones membra diuidentia and conceptus divisi. We shall therefore speak.
blocks.busolt-s25-001: These contain two concepts of things, and in them a distinction is made
blocks.busolt-s25-002: a.) The subject is the concept of which the other is a mark, or est conceptus, quem per alium cognitio.
blocks.busolt-s25-003: b.) The predicate is a concept that is a mark of the other, or est conceptus per quem subiectum repraesento cognitione.
blocks.busolt-s25-004: c.) The copula is that by which the relation of the conceptuum is designated.
blocks.busolt-s25-005: Categorical judgments are divided, quoad qualitatem, into affirmatiua negatiua and infinita
blocks.busolt-s25-006: a.) Judicium affirmatiuum, when the copula est expresses the connection of the subject and predicate.
blocks.busolt-s25-007: b.) Judicium negatiuum, when the copula non est is the opposition of the subject and predicate, or the negation of the judgment; it is therefore expressed through the negation of the relation, so the negation must stand with the copula and not with the predicate: for if the latter happens, then the concept is indeed negating but not the judgment: for in judgments logic looks merely to the relation
blocks.busolt-s25-008: Judicium infinitum when the predicate is negated; quoad quantitatem into universalia particularia, et singularia.
blocks.busolt-s25-009: 1.) Judicium universale ubi praedicatum de tota Sphaera praedicatur.
blocks.busolt-s25-010: 2.) Judicium particulare vbi praedicatum de parte Sphaerae praedicatur.
blocks.busolt-s25-011: 3.) Judicium singulare ubi Subiectum caret Sphaera ideoque praedicatum de toto subiecto praedicatur.
blocks.busolt-s25-012: The judicia singularia can be considered as judicia vniversalia, insofar as the predicate holds of the subject without exception, and for that reason the judicia singularia are also rightly omitted by most. One also speaks of generalia and specialia, but generalia are not universalia, and specialia are not particularia. E.g. To present geography generaliter does not mean to present it vniversaliter. For geography holds only particulariter of the earth. Generalia quae ad genus pertinent et specialia, quae ad speciem pertinent. Some judgments are so constituted that one must restrict the concept of the subject in order for the judgment to be valid. E.g. All angles in a triangle together make up 180 degrees; but that holds only of rectilinear triangles, not of curvilinear ones. Likewise, all bodies are heavy; but if there is no other body there by which it can orient itself, how can it be heavy? Thus this concept too must be restricted in relation to another body. In such judgments, therefore, the subject, or better the universality of the subject, must be restricted so that this predicate belongs to it. Judgments of this kind, where the assertion is conditioned, are called conditioned judgments. But if the condition is placed not with the subject but with the copula, the judgment is called judicium modale, e.g. All bodies are heavy contingently; from this arises the so-called modalitas iudiciorum, in which there occur: possibility, actuality, necessity. Remark: This modality is of the highest importance: for how often are possibility and necessity not confused with one another. E.g. In the demonstration of the immortality of the soul. To express the judgments of quality and quantity, letters have been chosen, which is of no use here, only in syllogistic, namely: Aßerit A, negat E, sed vniversaliter ambo Aßerit I, negat O, sed particulariter ambo.
blocks.busolt-s25-013: The logicians express modality through the question Quae propositio? Quality through Qualis est propositio? Quantity through Quanta est propositio.
blocks.busolt-s25-014: Up to here we have spoken of simple judgments, but there are also composite judgments. E.g. God, the soul and all finite
blocks.busolt-s25-015: spirits are immortal. Composite judgments rest on the fact that either
blocks.busolt-s26-001: Hypothetical judgments consist of two judgments which have a relation of the consequens, and to this belongs
blocks.busolt-s26-002: a. Antecedens, or that which precedes the consequence; that is the ground.
blocks.busolt-s26-003: b. Consequens, or that which follows from the antecedens; that is the consequence. They therefore have a relation of the nexus of judgments. Disjunctive judgments consist of two or more judgments which have a relation of opposition, which opposition, however, must be contradictory; the membra must therefore be contradictory, but together equal to the Conceptus diuersus.
blocks.busolt-s26-004: An exponible judgment is one that is at once affirming and negating. In German the words only, few, etc. etc. serve for such judgments, e.g. Few human beings are pious, some human beings are pious, some are not pious. Aesthetic judgments we distinguish from logical ones by there being, besides the concepts, also a sensation, e.g. Oh! How many human beings are godless! This is an aesthetic judgment. If we accept a proposition as practical, we can say: it is formaliter practical, and then it is opposed to the theoretical; or it is materialiter practical, and then it is opposed to the speculative. According to form, practical propositions are those according to which an exercise is possible; here it is not the relation of cognitions but the relation of freedom. These practical propositions are opposed to the theoretical. E.g. A triangle consists of three straight lines; this is theoretical. To describe a triangle from three given straight lines is formally practical. Of such practical propositions as are opposed to the speculative, logic knows nothing.
blocks.busolt-s26-005: A cognition theoretical according to form, from which many propositions can be derived that I ought to do, or which contains many imperatives, is practical according to matter. E.g. There is a single judge of the world. But logic, which abstracts from all content, knows nothing of the fact that some cognitions are so fruitful. The practical propositions in logic must be: to make an inference from given judgments and a terminus medius. The author speaks of demonstrable and indemonstrable judgments. Demonstrable judgments are those before which a judgment must precede, or which require a proof for the confirmation of their truth. Indemonstrable judgments are those which need no proof at all, but are true in themselves. The first are mediately certain, the others immediately certain judgments. We often say a proposition is immediately certain when it is not. Hence one must first assume a judgment to be mediately certain, because we
blocks.busolt-s26-006: a.) Perhaps also sense the result of the proof in us but do not have the proof itself.
blocks.busolt-s26-007: b.) Because the human understanding is more inclined to assume something as mediately certain. For it always wants to go further; we must therefore handle these propositions carefully, and examine them closely at first.
blocks.busolt-s26-008: The author calls an unexaminable cognition empty, because through it our cognition increases by nothing, nor loses anything. But there can be a cognition
blocks.busolt-s26-009: a.) Empty in sense, i.e. a proposition that is empty according to matter.
blocks.busolt-s26-010: b.) Empty according to the form of the understanding, e.g. The human being has a human essence.
blocks.busolt-s26-011: These propositions that explain idem per idem advance cognition neither analytically nor synthetically; they are tautological propositions; through them I have neither an increase in distinctness nor an addition to cognition. But not all identical propositions are empty propositions; only the tautological ones. An identical proposition that can be seen only through analysis is not to be regarded as an empty proposition: for it helps toward distinctness. According to content a proposition is empty if its representations relate to no subject. The identity in tautology is cognized immediately, but proper identity mediately, i.e. through the setting apart of the concepts. These tautological propositions neither help nor harm. But we perceive even what is true as absurd if it is conducive to none of our purposes. Negating propositions do not indeed extend our cognitions, but they remedy errors, whereas false propositions harm. E.g. The soul is not composite. If I use something negatively which no one has ever called in doubt, it becomes absurd.
blocks.busolt-s26-012: Propositiones indemonstrabiles are hypothetical propositions which have arisen not through dissection of the subject but from elsewhere. Synthetic propositions a priori, if they are intuitive a priori, are axiomata. Philosophy has no false judgments a priori, but insofar as it is discursive, philosophy does have principia axiomata. Axiom means as much as a dignity that is distinct in itself, and need not be proved; it already brings certainty with it. The author treats Judicia intuitiua and discursiua.
blocks.busolt-s26-013: a.) Judicia intuitiua are, when they represent something concrete in singulari.
blocks.busolt-s26-015: 1.) A priori intuitive, i.e. pure intuiting concepts (iudicia), mathematical.
blocks.busolt-s26-017: A consectarium is a proposition of inference, especially in philosophy. A corollarium is a proposition from which the other is inferred by an inference, especially in mathematics. Corollarium est ratio cinatio monosyllogistica. A theorem is a theoretical proposition insofar as it is capable of and requires a proof. It is nothing other than a est ratio cinatio polysyllogistica, i.e. a proposition that is inferred from other preceding inferences. The requisites of the theorem are.
blocks.busolt-s26-020: A problema is a practical proposition, distinguished from the preceding. For the requisites of the problem are:
blocks.busolt-s26-021: a.) Quaestio Problematis per quod exponitur, quid fieri debeat.
blocks.busolt-s26-022: b.) Resolutio quaestionis, quo modo fieri debeat.
blocks.busolt-s26-023: c.) Demonstratio, hanc resolutionem esse veram
blocks.busolt-s26-024: These tasks belong especially in mathematics, yet there are also special ones, as in morals, in medicine, in the human soul.
blocks.busolt-s26-025: It is therefore a very important rule: ne sit tautologica problematis resolutio, i.e. ne resolutionem praedicamus in definitionem. In morals there are therefore, as said, too many such problematic resolutions; this comes precisely from the fact that morals as canon is already actually there, i.e. that we actually have rules by which we direct the judgments of the understanding, and appraisals of moral actions, but not as organon, i.e. morals has not yet been presented so that the concepts of the understanding flow into my will and inclination, so that virtue is not merely approved but also practised. In the tautological resolution of the problem one analyses the definition itself; in morals the treatise need not be precisely precise, but in mathematics no abundance can take place; for although otherwise precision is an essential property of a system, some sciences are nevertheless exempted from it, and to these belong, besides morals, also the physical sciences
blocks.busolt-s26-026: 1. Definitiones axiomata corollaria, theoremata cum suis demonstrationibus, problemata etiam resolutionibus et demonstrationibus, hae sunt partes systematis eiusdemque dogmatici.
blocks.busolt-s26-027: But the following belongs to such a dogmatic system:
blocks.busolt-s26-028: a.) Partes domesticae quae constituent proprie systemam.
blocks.busolt-s26-029: b.) Partes peregrinae quae quasi alio ex campo depromuntur, vbi in morali Philosophia de existentia Dei, ita in metaphysicis, exempla ex physicis desumuntur eiusmodi pars vocatur lemma, quod est pars systematis peregrinae alia ex scientia exercita.
blocks.busolt-s26-031: a.) Partes essentiales sunt quibus sublatis totum tollitur systema.
blocks.busolt-s26-032: b.) Partes extra essentiales, quibus illustratur haec alienae systematis pars non extenditur; tale est Notion. That is properly the resting place of the system; in it one mentions the history, the utility of the system, one refutes the opponents in it. They are for the most part aesthetic.
blocks.busolt-s26-033: Qualitaet nulla in logicis dicitur, vbi ignorantiae scrutantis proceßio, pro ipsius rei definitione causaeque inventione sumitur e.g. quae nam est causa propagationis animalium, plantarumque? resp.: vis plastica. Here I define idem per idem, and it is said just as much as: The cause of this effect is hidden. What does a cognition gain after such an answer?
blocks.busolt-s26-034: Remark: Qualitas occulta est Tautologica phaenomenorum explicatio et enim subiectum respicit, non Obiectum. Eiusmodi est ideosyncrasia Lamberti, cuius ait hominis sibi propinquam habitum cane et angue aversantem. Et vero ideosyncrasia quali, quae in hoc illudere indiuiduum influit. Of just this kind is the word called in more recent times bon sens (healthy understanding). For who has given a definition of sensus communis, unless it be tautological? Even the Crusian philosophy rests on a principle that is nothing other than a qualitas occulta, namely: what I find to be nothing other than true, that is true. The Newtonian philosophy, which is grounded on the principle of the reciprocal sphere in the connection of the course of the world, takes the word vis attractiva for a qualitas occulta in the physical sense, that is merely as a confession of ignorance of the true causes, but not for the true cause itself.
blocks.busolt-s26-035: If a judgment is inferred from another without an intermediate judgment, then this is an inference of the understanding; per iudicium intermedium an inference of reason, e.g. All human beings are mortal, therefore Caius too is mortal. Here Caius is a concept that I did not have before; it is therefore inferred falsely, and I must infer only mediately, by making for myself a concept of Caius. For the consequentia immediata, iudicium praeuium and exclusio must retain a concept. They are not distinguished otherwise than only in quality, quantity and relation. The consequentiae immediatae occur
blocks.busolt-s26-041: The first kind can be dropped; it is empty, because it is as good as nothing to infer one from the other what is the same as the former; it always remains the same judgment. In the second kind I infer from the universal to the particular. In the third kind one is to infer immediately per iudicia opposita. This opposition is threefold.
blocks.busolt-s26-042: a.) Contradictory; here of two judgments only one can be true, and I therefore infer: if one is true, the other is false, and conversely. For this it is required that one be universal affirmative and the other particular negative, or that one be universal negative and the other particular affirmative. E.g. All human beings are mortal, some are not mortal. No substance is simple, some are simple:
blocks.busolt-s26-043: b.) Subcontrary, where one judgment is particular affirmative and the other particular negative, e.g. Some human beings are evil, – some are not evil.
blocks.busolt-s26-044: c.) Contrary, when a universal negative judgment is opposed to a universal affirmative judgment, or conversely, e.g. All human beings are vicious. Over against such a proposition the other can be set so that he says: No human being is vicious. Here he does more than is necessary to contradict the other. Judicia contraria opposita can both be false, because more is denied in them than is necessary. The falsity therefore lies in the universality. In the following kinds one alters the subject and predicate, but in conversion one can alter the quantity, but not the quality. The transposition of the terms is called metathesis terminorum. Through this arises an immediate inference through the conversion of judgments, where the quantity is transposed and not the quality, and through the contraposition of judgments, where the quality is transposed and not the quantity. E.g. All human beings are mortal; some mortals are therefore human beings, i.e. through conversion. What is not mortal is no human being, i.e. through contraposition. In the conversion of judgments the judgment that is to be turned about is called: judicium conversum; that through which the conversion arises, iudicium convertens. The conversion occurs either per accidens or simpliciter.
blocks.busolt-s26-045: The conditions according to form are these;
blocks.busolt-s26-046: a.) Universal affirmative propositions can be converted only per accidens, universal negative propositions only simpliciter, and thirdly particular affirmative or negative propositions can also be converted simpliciter. The first means as much as: iudicium conuersum est vniversale, and of these I can now say conversely: some mortals are human beings. I namely think of mortals among whom are also the human beings, i.e. the subject human being is under the sphere of the mortals, as of the predicate. The predicate must therefore be greater than the subject; I can therefore take some mortals for human beings. There are universal affirmative propositions that can be converted simpliciter, in which the sphere of the subject and predicate is equal, e.g. All figures enclosed by three straight lines are triangles, all triangles are figures enclosed by three straight lines, are three-corners, i.e. a subtlety, and I leave it here to each to decide how much he wants to take out of an infinite multitude of three-corners. This difference, however, is evanescent. All negative judgments that contain a conflict can be converted simpliciter, e.g. no triangle is without angles, no figure without angles is a triangle; all particular affirmative or negative propositions can be converted simpliciter, i.e. so that the quantity is not altered. Contraposition means as much as: every universal proposition can be contraposed. E.g. All human beings are mortal, non-mortals are not human beings. How is inference made according to the judicia mediata? If one concept is to be inferred from another that is not contained in the former, one must add a concept that contains the condition of the rule; the concept of the object now contains the condition of the rule, and so the predicate of the conclusion must also hold of this conclusion. E.g. All human beings are mortal, Caius is a human being, therefore Caius is mortal. This inference of reason is grounded on the principle: to every thing, insofar as it can be subsumed under the condition, the predicate belongs; an inference of reason, however, is cognitio a priori per subsumtionem conceptus sub conditione regulae cuiusdam generali.
blocks.busolt-s26-047: The inference of reason has two requisites
blocks.busolt-s26-048: a.) General rule, i.e. the major.
blocks.busolt-s26-049: b.) The subsumption of a concept under the condition of this general rule, i.e. the minor.
blocks.busolt-s26-050: c.) The connection of the predicate with the subject, or that which accrues from the general rule of the subsumption; this is the conclusion. Major and minor are called premises. The premises and the conclusion are therefore what belongs to the inference.
blocks.busolt-s26-051: In these inferences one looks to relation, and according to this the inferences are divided into categorical, hypothetical and disjunctive. All inferences are assessed according to the maior propositio. If that is a categorical judgment, the inference is also categorical. Only in categorical inferences are there subject, predicate and terminus medius, and hence one readily sees the importance of the saying: for an inference of reason 3 termini are required: the major, or the predicate of the conclusion, the minor, or the subject of the conclusion, and the terminus medius, which is the condition of the conclusion; every inference of reason consists in general of 3 parts.
blocks.busolt-s26-055: The matter of inferences of reason is the premises, or propositions from which the conclusion follows. The form consists in the inference of the conclusion from the premises. An inference of reason can be correct in matter but fail in form. Only in categorical inferences is there a medius terminus. In hypothetical ones there is merely the relation of two judgments, how one follows from the correctness of the other.
blocks.busolt-s27-001: Among the chief rule of inferences of reason others otherwise count the principle of contradiction: No judgment is true where the predicate contradicts the subject. But this principium of contradiction cannot be used as an inference of reason: for it is only a principium iudicii.
blocks.busolt-s27-002: An inference of reason is affirmative when the conclusion is affirmative, and negative when the conclusion is negative. According to this general division of all inferences of reason we make 2 particular rules:
blocks.busolt-s27-003: a.) Nota notae est Nota rei ipsius; this holds of affirmative judgments.
blocks.busolt-s27-004: b.) Repugnans notae repugnat rei ipsi; this holds of negative inferences, e.g. Being changeable is a mark of everything divisible, being divisible is a mark of a body, therefore by means of divisibility changeability is a mark of the body.
blocks.busolt-s27-005: Every conclusion contains subject and predicate; the terminus medius occurs in both premises; thus in the maior there will be the predicate and terminus medius, in the minor the subject and terminus medius. In such inferences of reason only the terminus medius can be transposed. The manner of transposition is fourfold, and hence arise precisely the 4 figures of syllogistic.
blocks.busolt-s27-006: Repugnans notae repugnat rei ipsi. E.g. Nothing composite is simple, all matter is composite, therefore no matter is simple, etc. Being simple holds of composites, and by virtue of the composite of bodies. The two rules cited are just what the dictum de omni et nullo was for the ancients.
blocks.busolt-s27-007: a.) Dictum de omni quidquid valet de genere aut specie valet etiam de omnibus indiuiduis in genere aut specie contentis.
blocks.busolt-s27-008: b.) Dictum de nullo quidquid repugnat generi aut speciei, repugnat etiam omnibus indiuiduis in genere aut specie contentis.
blocks.busolt-s27-009: The principle of hypothetical and disjunctive inferences the author explains in §§ 364 and 365. There are therefore only three principles of inferences of reason; for the consequentiae immediatae are properly not inferences of reason; they are only consequences and need no rule. The author speaks of ordinary and extraordinary inferences of reason. But there is in this no other difference than that the inferences in which the form is hidden are extraordinary.
blocks.busolt-s28-001: Figura I. Est notior quam ut egeat explicatione, est quasi radi x omnis conversionis medii Termini in ceteris.
blocks.busolt-s28-002: Figura II. Hic medius Terminus est praedicatum in maiori et minori e.g. No thinking being is composite, all bodies are composite, therefore no body is a thinking being.
blocks.busolt-s28-003: Figura III. Hic medius Terminus in maiori et minori propositione est Subiectum. E.g. All human beings are imperfect; some human beings are virtuous, therefore some virtuous ones are imperfect.
blocks.busolt-s28-004: Figura IV. Hic medius Terminus est Praedicatum in maiori et Subiectum in minori E.g. Quidquid habet vim agendi est Spiritus omnis spiritus est substantia, ergo omnis substantia habet vim agendi.
blocks.busolt-s29-001: 1.) In an ordinary inference of reason there can be no more than 3 principal concepts; for the conclusion has only 2. Remark: If one of the two principal concepts in the premises is ambiguous, the ambiguity is found in the whole inference. E.g. In the place where I am there is no other; the room is the place where I am; therefore in the room there is no other.
blocks.busolt-s29-002: 2.) Medius Terminus ne ingrediatur conclusionem, id vero pessimi concurrit vitium.
blocks.busolt-s29-003: 3.) Ex puris negatiuis nihil sequitur. One sees this through healthy reason; it follows from the nature of the thing itself: for the subsumption must be under the condition of the rule. I must say that to a thing belongs what is the condition of the rule, and this must surely be affirmative. E.g. No human being is an irrational animal, no ox is a human being, therefore no ox is an irrational animal.
blocks.busolt-s29-004: 4.) Ex puris particularibus nihil sequitur. Because otherwise what stands under the condition of the rule cannot be applied to its predicate. E.g. Some sentient beings are human beings, some irrational animals are sentient beings, therefore some irrational animals are human beings.
blocks.busolt-s29-005: 5.) Conclusio sequi debet partem debiliorem. NB: Among the premises, that is called the pars debilior which is either particular or negative. The proposition runs: if one premise is negative, the conclusion is negative; if one premise is particular, the conclusion is particular. Ground: If I have subsumed only some things under the condition of the general rule, then the predicate of the general rule too must hold only of some; if the rule is negative, then the negation of the rule must also hold of what stands under the rule.
blocks.busolt-s29-006: 6.) In Conclusione nec Plus, nec Minus continentur quam in praemissis id est, ne notus in conclusione amplus reperiatur. Thus no more must be inferred than what is comprehended in the premises. In the praemissis there are maior, minor and Terminus medius. In the conclusion only maior and minor. The first figure is immediately evident. In the second and third figure one must first reflect what the consequence would be. The fourth figure the logicians have called the unnatural one; with this they evidently noticed the entanglement. In the last figures the form can be hidden very well.
blocks.busolt-s29-007: The rules of the first figure are:
blocks.busolt-s29-010: These rules seem to restrict the first figure, but they show us rather its extension to each and every kind of inference; the major must by virtue of the rule be universal, but it can also be affirmative or negative; the minor is to be affirmative, but it can also be universal and particular. Thus in the first figure inferences of every quality and quantity are possible, thus of A, E, I, et O. In the others only some of them are ever possible; consequently the first figure is the genuine, the only natural and pure one. Remark: The above rules hold for each and every inference of reason: for in every inference of reason there must always be a rule, but a rule is nothing other than a universal truth. Further, since in every inference of reason I am to subsume a concept, I must indeed assert that this concept belongs under a universal rule; hence affirm.
blocks.busolt-s29-011: The rules of the second figure are restricted merely to one kind of inferences, namely to negative conclusions!
blocks.busolt-s29-012: The third figure can have only particular conclusions.
blocks.busolt-s29-013: In the fourth figure only particular or negative conclusions are possible; the conclusion thus has only partes debiliores. From this it is evident that the first figure alone is the pure one, but that all the others have mixed inferences. Ratiocinium purum is where, besides the major, the minor and the conclusion, no other proposition enters in.
blocks.busolt-s29-014: Ratiocinium impurum seu hybridum, where a consequentia immediata must be thought along with the 3 propositions. It is thus a mating of a ratiocinium with a consequentia immediata; this occurs in the last three figures. The explanation from the second figure: no thinking being is composite, all bodies are composite, therefore no body is a thinking substance. – Here, in considering the major, I think to myself per conversionem: nothing composite is a thinking substance; I therefore bring the second figure into the first per conuersionem maioris. The first conclusion must here be negative, for the second is to be brought into the first per conversionem; in this the major must be universal, so since only negative propositions can yield a universal proposition per conversionem simpliciter, the conclusion must also be negative: Conclusio sequitur partem debiliorem.
blocks.busolt-s29-015: Explanation of the third figure: All human beings are imperfect, some are virtuous; therefore some virtuous are imperfect. Here the terminus medius does not stand in its proper place, and only the reduction into the first figure gives it this. All human beings are imperfect, some virtuous are human beings, therefore some virtuous are imperfect. In reductione igitur tertiae Figurae metathesis Terminorum efficit minorem quae quidem per consequentiam immediatam. From some virtuous are human beings, it follows, some human beings are virtuous. The proof of the third figure, namely that only particular conclusions occur in it, lies in this, that I must be able to reduce the minor here into the first figure, but this minor must be affirmative; so it is necessary, since particular propositions can always be simply converted per conseqventiam immediatam, that a particular proposition also be in the minor proposition, and then, in accordance with this as the pars debilior, the inference is correct; hence the conclusion in the third figure must always be particular.
blocks.busolt-s29-016: In the fourth figure the major is made into the minor; but from this it is now evident that the last 3 kinds of inference are unnatural and merely confuse the understanding, and hence must be banished from logic, which is supposed to be a lighthouse of the soul; every judgment has a modus, which expresses the quantity and quality; the vowels A, E, I, O signify such. Of these four vowels only 3 can occur in a syllogism, because there are only 3 propositions.
blocks.busolt-s29-017: From the transposition of these vowels arise 64 particular forms. But through the rule ex puris negatiuis nihil sequitur 16 drop out, through conclusio sequitur partem debiliorem 24 drop out; altogether there are only 19 possible ones, among which some are corrupt, so that only remain. To bring these into formulas, a certain technique of artificial words has been devised. In doing so, consonants have been added to the vowels, which, however, are all arbitrary as well. The rules of the vowels are:
blocks.busolt-s29-018: a.) S vult simpliciter verti, P vero accidens. M vult transponi, this happens per Metathesin, per migrationem.
blocks.busolt-s29-019: b.) C per impossibili duci, per contrapositionem, the artificial words are called
blocks.busolt-s29-020: In the first figure Barbara, Celarent, Darii, Ferio. In the second figure Cesare, Camestres, Festino, Barocco. In the third figure Darapti, Felapton, Disamis, Datisi, Bocardo, Ferison. In the fourth figure Calemes, Bamalip, Dimatis, Fesapo, Fresisom. All of this that has been said so far about syllogisms holds only of categorical inferences. The hypothetical Ratiocinia are of an entirely different kind. The Ratiocinia hypothetica have 2 Modos:
blocks.busolt-s29-021: a.) Modum ponentem. Here I infer a veritate antecedentis ad consequentis positionem.
blocks.busolt-s29-022: b.) Modum tollentem; here I infer a remotione consequentis ad remotionem antecedentis, e.g. if there is a blind chance, then there is no order in the world atqui falsum est posterius ergo primus; id est modus tollens.
blocks.busolt-s29-023: If bodies are divisible, then they are changeable; atqui verum est prius, ergo posterius.
