The major propositionis says nothing more than how one proposition follows from the other. If the consequens is incorrect, one says it is inferred a baculo ad angulum. The modus tollens occurs only a consequente ad antecedentem, namely sublato consequente tollitur antecedens, but a positione consequentis ad positionem antecedentis non valet modus ponens. The disjunctive inferences of reason consist in this, that the major is divided into several parts which are opposed to one another.
blocks.busolt-s29-024: The membra diuidentia we call, in an inference of reason, membra disiunctiua. In such an inference we infer a negatigatione omnium membrorum disiunctionis praeter vnum ad positionem huius vnius
blocks.busolt-s29-025: With two Membra one infers a negatione vnius ad positionem alterius. If one is false, then the other is true. Or I also infer a positione vnius membri disiunctionis ad negationem ceterorum omnium.
blocks.busolt-s29-026: Dilemma est id argumentandi genus, in quo maior est hypothetica. All dilemmata have a negative conclusion, e.g. If God has not created the best world, then he either could not have created it, or did not want to create it. Dicitur alius Syllogismus cornutus crocodilus. That the ancients made much of the dilemma, when they drew other consequences from the assertions. A dilemma always has something sophistical about it, and is a modus indirectus of inferring.
blocks.busolt-s29-028: From the consequence to the ground, for the proposition is then not an affirmation, because a consequence can have more than one ground. Only then can I infer with truth according to this modus, if I confirm the truth of all the consequences as true. To infer from the falsity of the consequences to the falsity of the ground is quite easy, for I need only show that one consequence is false. The dilemma has much that is convenient about it: for
blocks.busolt-s29-029: a.) One does not prove directly, from the constitution of the thing
blocks.busolt-s29-030: b.) Negative propositions also have more emphasis. They serve, as it were, for conviction. A contradiction always makes a greater relative impression; it is much more striking than a true proof; what holds of immediate consequences has just been said. Every Ratiocinium is either formal or crypticum, a concealed inference of reason. We speak for the most part through Ratiocinia cryptica. E.g. The soul, because it is simple, is imperishable. A Ratiocinium formale is that which is in accordance with the schools. In the understanding every Ratiocinium is formale, in the words not always. An enthymema is called an inference where one omits one of the premises, e.g. All human beings can err, therefore I.
blocks.busolt-s29-031: The inferences through induction and through analogy. The inferences of reason are either apodictic or not. What I cognize through reason is apodictic. I cognize through it everything that is necessary; what I cognize, on the other hand, through experience is not apodictic. The inferences of the understanding give merely an empirical certainty, yet an empirical certainty can be called necessity, namely if it helps toward the use in experience as much as a necessity. Those are strict, these not strict inferences. In inferences of reason we derive the particular from the universal; in inferences of the understanding the universal from the particular. The former is Ratiocinium genuinum, the latter spurium, which the author calls ordinaire extraordinis. But because nothing follows from purely particular propositions, the understanding is concerned to make rules here through its perceptions, i.e. universal propositions. Thus, e.g., I see merely through experience that all human beings must die, because namely this one, that one and all human beings who have lived have died: I thus infer here conversely, as in the ratiocinia. What belongs to so many individuals as have ever existed, that belongs to all others of this kind, i.e. what we call induction. This is the path that the understanding continually takes. Meanwhile there is no apodictic certainty here: for individual cases can still always make exceptions to our so-called rules, as, e.g., some human bodies are still found where the heart beats on the right side, and altogether everything lies reversed. Notwithstanding this, the physician does not change his laudana. It is just so with all languages and with the general character of nations, as one says, e.g.: that all people in France are polite, only the innkeepers not, and conversely in England all are coarse, only the innkeepers polite; on the whole the rule nulla regula sine exceptione belongs here. These exceptions are called instances in disputing; the rule then has only an actuality in inferring in experience, and there an exception can be, provided only that the whole magnitude is not cancelled. Through induction we make universal propositions, and this inference is a particulaire ad vniversale. Otherwise there is also a kind of induction from systematic propositions, i.e. when something is predicated of a genus because it already lies in the analysis of the concept itself. E.g. Man is rational. There is yet a second way of inferring obliquely, namely through analogy. This kind of inference is distinguished from the previous one in that, if two things have in common as many items as I have perceived through the most careful investigation, they can also agree in all the items that I cannot yet investigate. I thus do not bring my inference to several judgments but to properties of just these same things. Thus we infer the circulation of the blood in animals from the otherwise existing similarity of the human and animal body in their constitution. Likewise the inner structure of polyps, in which we otherwise notice no entrails. These inferences through induction and analogy are, as it were, the two crutches of human ratiocination, true crutches, for we go very unsurely along; it is a mere attempt. You say, e.g., all young either come into the world alive or are hatched from eggs. Notwithstanding this, it was always known that in polyps there are young in every severed part. Sophisma is a dialectical kind of inference that has merely the semblance of truth. The semblance can lie
blocks.busolt-s29-032: a.) In the matter, i.e. in praemißis or in the propositions themselves, or
blocks.busolt-s29-033: b.) In the form, i.e. when the semblance lies in the conclusion (in the way of inferring).
blocks.busolt-s29-034: Of the former we do not speak here; some dialecticians amused themselves with the second, others with the first. Such an inference is called a paralogical one when, e.g., a terminus is ambiguous, e.g. No artist is born. The ancients had such an inference, which they called the Liar: if you say you lie and speak the truth, then you speak the truth if you lie. Sophisma heterogenea, vbi Status quaestionis mutatur, dicitur etiam Sophisma ignorationis elenchi Hic pertinet illud alter mulget hircum, alter supponit cribrum. Copulative sophisms are those in which properly two syllogisms are combined, as: Everything simple is immortal, God and all spirits are simple.
blocks.busolt-s29-035: The ars Polysyllogistica is when we chain many inferences together, and the conclusion of the preceding inference becomes in it the premise of the following one, and we here always infer in Episyllogisms, and so the Polysyllogistic is progrediens; but if I go back to the deduction and prove one of the premises, the Polysyllogistic is regrediens. This otherwise seems to be applied advantageously, especially in disputing; but great caution is necessary in it, for if in the Polysyllogistic progrediens I concede the first premise and do not properly examine its correctness in matter and form, true things can always be inferred which, however, stand as well as fall with the premise. So that no error occur in disputing in this, it is advisable that the conclusion of the Opponent always give the assertion of the Respondent. The mentioned error in progredient syllogisms has not seldom crept into philosophical systems. The regredient Syllogistic, by contrast, has far greater advantages over the first: for I examine critically here whether the ground is true and the consequence correct. Sorites is merely an inference of the expression. There I heap conclusion upon conclusion and leave out the premises. Such a chaining of inferences can now consist of categorical or hypothetical propositions, and so it becomes Sorites categoricus, Sorites Hypotheticus. Circulus in demonstrando, saltus in probando occurs when I infer a ratione remota immediately ad rationatum. The consequence is thus not clear here, and I leave out a necessary intermediate inference.
blocks.busolt-s29-036: Petitio Principii. Petere Principium means to beg a principium, postulare principium is to demand that one be allowed to prove it to him. A proof that demonstrates too little is therefore to be regarded not as false but as deficient, for I prove something, and something can still always be added. But a proof that proves too much is false and proves nothing at all.
blocks.busolt-s30-001: The Topica of Aristotle were nothing other than a review of all the titles and argumenta under which objects can be considered; as, e.g., we can consider a thing from various points of view. Locus topicus is a so-called title in logic under which an object can be considered and treated. I can consider a thing in genere and in differentia specifica, according to distinctness and indistinctness; as ground and consequence, as axiom and theorem etc. Thus a metaphysical passage is Locus metaphysicus loci rerum sunt etiam fines rerum. There are loci grammatici; there I can consider an object according to its definition. These Loci Logici, because they concern only the form, are called common kinds, Loci communes or better common propositions. Locorum communium vsus et in logicis et in rhetoricis locum habet. Loci ethici deals with decore and honesto; Loci physici, whether I derive a thing from causis efficientibus or finalibus.
blocks.busolt-s31-001: Just as the theoretical part of logic sets out the general condition of the possible perfection of logical cognition, so practical logic is a general science which contains the condition for attaining to a possible logically perfect cognition. Here, then, the question is: how am I to attain to possible logical perfection in cognition, applying this here, that there? Here one should beware of tautological definitions: for for the most part one is accustomed to dispatch the solution thus: one should do what is required for it. Say instead: Acquaintance with the object at hand gives here the best solution. For here it depends on the matter alone, and not even practical logic can have this as its object. Only so far as belongs to the form can it teach us to apply all the rules of theory; thus only the application. The chief object of practical logic is accordingly method, i.e. the arrangement of manifold cognition with all logical perfection, insofar as it is to be taken together into a whole. Practical logic could accordingly also be called the pure general doctrine of method. Method is contradistinguished from manner. The latter requires merely the common manner of teaching, and everyone therefore has his manner, his taste, though popularity is the chief item in it. Manner is a way of treating the object according to laws of reason. Manner accordingly, like everything empirical, cannot be brought into rules. Yet popularity is the most praiseworthy property in it: for it presupposes logical perfection, since it is nothing other than accomodatio Logicae cognitionis ad sensum communem. One shows here, without any art, how our concepts expand gradually without scholastic rigor. Furthermore, manner and method are distinguished in that method belongs to science, manner merely to entertainment; just as the latter makes itself known through inclination and practice. In the latter even the faults are already beautiful: for it is nature; just as with women even the blemishes in the face make the beauty stand out the more.
blocks.busolt-s31-003: a.) The tumultuary, where one observes no order in thinking; yet in conceiving the tumultuary is permitted and advantageous;
blocks.busolt-s31-004: for one looks about, as it were, quite freely in the field of objects; whereas method sets limits for us in consideration: for the tumultuary serves manifoldness, method unity. This tumultuary in method is always a proof of a tumultuary way of thinking.
blocks.busolt-s31-005: b.) There is a kind of presentation which is rhapsodistic; by virtue of it one can always have observed an order in thinking, only one is not in a position to make the guiding thread of one's consideration visible. This reveals itself especially in the lack of titles of the sections; in short, the due right of method is lacking; for that makes things clear to one another.
blocks.busolt-s31-006: c.) A presentation is called aphoristic when, although method shines forth in thinking and even in the presentation, only the transition from one part to the other is not distinctly represented, when there is unity in thinking, but not continuity. The preceding chapter contains, as it were, no propaedeutic for the transition to the following; the aphorists surprise us, as it were, and not seldom become agreeable. Whereas a book of rhapsodistic method is unbearable, in that one cannot so soon look it up in the archive of memory. In the aphoristic method it is as if I leapt from one stone to another, which lie in a straight line.
blocks.busolt-s31-007: d.) Finally the popular method deserves, as the most generally useful, to be preferred to all others. For it is, as it were, the condescension of a man of science to common human understanding.
blocks.busolt-s31-008: The proper method has far too much exertion of the understanding, and then it forbids every kind of reconciliation. In popularity the French otherwise have the great advantage, and a Fontenelle can make a mathematical proposition just as comprehensible as an aesthetic truth. Method is also divided into the analytic and the synthetic. In the synthetic one goes from principles to principiata, in the other conversely; thus the whole of mathematics is synthetic. The analytic is, as it were, an inverse synthesis, and is philosophy. Furthermore method is divided:
blocks.busolt-s31-009: a.) Into the scientific; this belongs to scholars, and one looks in it especially to thoroughness. It presents everything in abstracto, namely order and distinctness are the chief work in it.
blocks.busolt-s31-010: b.) Into the popular; this looks also to the ideas, in that everything is presented in concreto. Thus Hume writes reflections on human understanding in scientific method, but with little applause. He treated this same matter in popular method, brought in comparisons from rhetoric, poetry, feeling etc. etc., and the book was approved throughout. Remark on the preceding. The synthetic method is suited only to the sciences where one goes from the universal to the particular, thus to mathematics; whereas in philosophy the analytic finds the most place, with the exception of some parts. The mathematical method is the proper method. Applying this same method to other sciences is merely in vain; otherwise one falls into the vice of method-mannerism. There is yet the division of method into:
blocks.busolt-s31-011: a.) Natural, namely objectively natural, which is adequate to the object. The method in concreto is a natural one
blocks.busolt-s31-012: b.) The artificial. If this artificial method is to have no fault, it must be nature; for art is really nothing other than cultivated nature. This is just what is called naivety, namely an art that seems nature, or a nature that seems art. Furthermore the syllogistic manner of teaching: there is none such, properly speaking, and it must not be tolerated either: for whom do formal inferences not annoy. Yet for individual propositions, in disputing, it is permitted. The tabular method is that where one sketches the skeleton of a system. The dialogical method instructs by discoursing. It is twofold:
blocks.busolt-s31-013: a.) Socratic, where the teacher poses as a pupil, and through analysis seeks to decide the question from the pupil himself. It is so called because Socrates in his dialogues made particular use of it.
blocks.busolt-s31-014: b.) Catechetical; this is merely for cognitions of memory, for there the teacher himself gives them to the pupil. The geographical method is that which presents the objects that are simultaneous.
blocks.busolt-s31-015: The chronological method is that which presents the objects that follow one another in time. There is yet the division into doctrine and discipline. Doctrine extends cognitions and is thus positive. Discipline merely holds off error, and is thus negative. Tumultuary meditation has much that is advantageous in it: for through this kind of foray, where from the footpath, without being held up, everywhere
blocks.busolt-s31-016: from every region we plunder, our cognition certainly gains not a little.
blocks.busolt-s32-001: In meditating one needs an object; consequently one must gather the materials, and this succeeds best through tumultuary thinking. To promote it further one peruses books, especially when it concerns historical or polemical matters; but otherwise the thinking of others gives us ourselves occasion for new ideas and for new thoughts.
blocks.busolt-s32-002: Lambert used lexica, and looked up synonyms, analogies etc. etc., and thus one obtains manifoldness. One observes this in thinking; in writing down, however, unity is required; the side thoughts that, as it were, spring up on the way, one notes in the margin, and afterwards divides them into their compartments. But because our imagination, once it has been set upon a journey, does not soon let go of it, one must, so as not always to consider the object from only one point of view, do oneself violence often to break off, to read books of an entirely different matter, and, as it were, to make a diuersion. In the morning one must bring the materials for a system into order, in the evening, on the other hand, gather materials: for in the evening the imagination roams about, as it were, occupied with many objects; in the morning, however, it is, as it were, under the supervision of reason.
blocks.busolt-s33-001: Speaking and talking are distinct. One speaks in order to make oneself understandable; one talks in order to attain one's end. How, then, is the philosopher to arrange his language? In general the philosopher looks more to the meaning of words than to style. The principium of this is: The expression must be adequate to the concept. He can therefore also use the language of scholars, that is not only a dead language, but also technical terms. Yet these are, so to speak, only an emergency nail, and he does not depart from common usage of language without deliberation and necessity; but for philosophical principles, with regard to expression, a language is seldom sufficient. German seems, along with Greek, to be the most philosophical; for it is the most correct of all, it has the most synonyms. Notwithstanding this, one seldom finds two words in the whole language that would be one and the same: for the multitude of synonyms is always a proof of the richness of a language. For by means of synonyms one can determine the different degrees of exactness in the object. The cause of the richness of the German language one fittingly derives from its missionaries, who, when they wanted to convert it, formed many of their already invented words after the Greek and Latin, as from compassio Mitleiden, misericordia Barmherzigkeit. Precisely because these missionaries, all improvers of the German language, wanted to enlighten the understanding of the Germans, they also had to speak little tropically, and therefore they had out of necessity to enrich the Romance language with quite new words, since otherwise these very tropes are a proof of the poverty of a language. Precisely when a language has many tropi, this gives occasion to various plays on words and witty conceits.
blocks.busolt-s33-002: Word-cutting is a great fault. To be sure one says verba valent sicut nummi, but only the high sovereign authority of the land has the right of coinage; otherwise, however, it remains true
